title: Investigating the star formation histories of galaxies from Cosmic Dawn to the Epoch of Reionization with the Santa Cruz SAM
comment: submitted to MNRAS, comments are welcome
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has opened a new window onto galaxy evolution in the very early Universe. In this work, we leverage halo merger trees extracted from the GUREFT dark-matter-only cosmological simulation suite together with the Santa Cruz semi-analytic model (SAM) for galaxy formation to investigate the predicted star formation histories (SFHs) of galaxies from cosmic dawn (z ~ 14) to the end of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR; z~6). While we find that on average, median SFHs of galaxies across all masses are uniformly and rapidly rising over time from 14 < z < 6 as expected, individual galaxy SFHs show a range of diverse SFHs, even for a fixed terminal mass or redshift, with bursts and mini-quenching episodes in agreement with SFHs inferred from observations. The median lookback time to form the youngest 50% (t_50) and 90% (t_90) of galaxies' stars decreases weakly with increasing stellar mass, and strongly with the redshift of observation. For galaxies at z>12, we find typical values of t_50 < 30 Myr and t_90 < 70 Myr, a factor of ~3 to 4 shorter than for comparable galaxies near the end of EoR (z ~ 6). The young-star dominated nature of stellar populations in ultra-high-z galaxies implies that careful modelling of young stellar populations is crucial for obtaining accurate synthetic photometry. In addition, our results have important implications for interpreting observational indicators of star formation histories and timescales.

AI.tldr: Using halo merger trees from the GUREFT simulation and the Santa Cruz semi-analytic model, the authors study galaxy star formation histories from z~14 to z~6. While median SFHs are uniformly rising, individual galaxies exhibit diverse SFHs with bursts and mini-quenching. Galaxies at z>12 have extremely young stellar populations (t_50 < 30 Myr, t_90 < 70 Myr), with implications for photometric modeling and observational indicators.
AI.motivation: To leverage JWST's new observational capabilities to understand galaxy evolution in the early Universe by investigating predicted star formation histories from cosmic dawn through the Epoch of Reionization.
AI.method: Halo merger trees from the GUREFT dark-matter-only cosmological simulation suite combined with the Santa Cruz semi-analytic model (SAM) for galaxy formation.
AI.result: Median SFHs rise uniformly across all masses from 14<z<6, but individual galaxies show diverse SFHs with bursts and mini-quenching. For z>12 galaxies, t_50 < 30 Myr and t_90 < 70 Myr, ~3-4x shorter than at z~6. Lookback time to form youngest stars decreases weakly with stellar mass and strongly with redshift.
AI.conclusion: Young-star dominated populations at ultra-high-z require careful modeling of young stellar populations for accurate synthetic photometry, with important implications for interpreting observational indicators of SFHs and timescales.

title: The largest sample of AGN outflows in dwarf galaxies using DESI DR1
comment: Submitted to MNRAS
summary: In the last decade, the presence of active galactic nuclei (AGN) outflows and feedback in dwarf galaxies ($\mathrm{M_\ast}$<$10^{10}\mathrm{M}_\odot$) has gained ground over supernova (SN) feedback as the main mechanism regulating star formation. In this work, we perform the first systematic search for AGN outflows in dwarf galaxies using the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Data Release 1 (DESI DR1). From $\sim$ 7 million galaxies at z$<$0.45, we identify ionized outflows through the detection of broad components in the [OIII]$\lambda5007$Åemission line. Galaxies are divided into dwarf and massive systems. Then, using emission-line diagnostic diagrams, we classify as star forming or AGN. We identify 1,502 AGN dwarf galaxies with outflow signatures. Comparing the distributions of star forming and AGN galaxies with outflows, we find that, among the 1,502 AGN dwarf galaxies with outflow signatures, AGN are the most likely drivers of the observed outflows in $\sim$83$\%$ of those with W$_{80}$ velocity $>250$ km s$^{-1}$. This constitutes the largest statistical sample of AGN outflows in dwarf galaxies to date. In massive galaxies, AGN dominance occurs above W$_{80}>350$ km s$^{-1}$. Therefore, two new velocity thresholds are proposed for identifying AGN-driven outflows in dwarf and massive galaxies. Besides, we find that outflows in dwarf galaxies are more likely to escape the dark matter halo than those in massive galaxies, allowing gas to be redistributed from the inner to the outer regions. This suggests that AGN outflows may have a major impact on dwarf galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using DESI DR1 data from ~7 million galaxies (z<0.45), the authors conducted the first systematic search for AGN outflows in dwarf galaxies (M*<10^10 M⊙), identifying 1,502 AGN dwarf galaxies with outflow signatures via broad [OIII]λ5007 components. AGN drive ~83% of outflows in dwarf galaxies at W80>250 km/s, compared to >350 km/s in massive galaxies. These outflows are more likely to escape dwarf galaxy halos, implying significant AGN feedback impact.
AI.motivation: To determine whether AGN outflows, rather than supernova feedback, are the dominant mechanism regulating star formation in dwarf galaxies, and to establish the first large statistical sample for studying such outflows.
AI.method: Analyzed ~7 million DESI DR1 galaxies at z<0.45; identified ionized outflows via broad [OIII]λ5007 emission line components; classified galaxies into dwarf vs. massive and star-forming vs. AGN using emission-line diagnostic diagrams; compared outflow velocity distributions (W80) between AGN and star-forming populations.
AI.result: 1,502 AGN dwarf galaxies with outflow signatures found; AGN drive ~83% of outflows in dwarfs at W80>250 km/s, while the threshold is W80>350 km/s for massive galaxies; dwarf galaxy outflows are more likely to escape the dark matter halo.
AI.conclusion: AGN outflows are the dominant driver of fast outflows in dwarf galaxies, with lower velocity thresholds than in massive galaxies, and can significantly impact dwarf galaxy evolution by redistributing gas beyond the halo.

title: Polar coordinate transformations for machine learning based dark matter subhalo detection in strong gravitational lenses
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures
summary: Strong gravitational lensing provides a powerful probe of dark matter, particularly on small scales where the gravitational effects of dark matter subhalos within galaxies can manifest as perturbations within the extended arcs of gravitationally lensed sources. We investigate whether transforming lensed images into polar coordinates improves the ability of convolutional neural networks to infer subhalo mass. We introduce a machine learning architecture that outputs a prediction uncertainty alongside a mass prediction to enable assessment of network reliability. Using simulated Hubble Space Telescope observations, we compare our models trained on Cartesian and polar representations under different initialisation schemes, noise levels, and subhalo concentrations ($c=60$, $c=30$). We find that polar-transformed inputs consistently yield higher subhalo detection fractions than standard Cartesian images across all tested masses. For subhalos with mass $10^9M_\odot \leq M \leq 10^{9.5}M_\odot$, the fraction of subhalos the network is able to detect increases by $\sim 15$ per cent. Pretrained networks outperform randomly initialized networks, and the polar transform consistently improves network performance in both low signal-to-noise data and for lower-concentration subhalos. The relative improvement is highest in regimes where subhalo perturbations are most difficult to detect, such as low signal-to-noise data or systems containing low concentration subhalos. These results demonstrate that presenting strong lensing images in a polar representaion provides a computationally inexpensive way of improving CNN-based subhalo detection.

AI.tldr: Using polar-transformed coordinates in CNNs improves subhalo detection in strong gravitational lensing images by ~15% compared to standard Cartesian inputs, particularly for low-mass, low-concentration subhalos and noisy data.
AI.motivation: Strong gravitational lensing probes dark matter subhalos on small scales, but detecting their subtle perturbations in lensed arcs is challenging. The authors investigate whether transforming lensed images to polar coordinates can improve CNN-based subhalo mass inference.
AI.method: A CNN architecture with prediction uncertainty is trained on simulated HST observations. Models are compared across Cartesian vs. polar representations, different initialization schemes, noise levels, and subhalo concentrations (c=60, c=30).
AI.result: Polar-transformed inputs yield ~15% higher detection fractions for subhalos with mass 10^9–10^9.5 M☉. Pretrained networks outperform random initialization. Polar transform improves performance in low-SNR data and for lower-concentration subhalos, with greatest relative gains in the most challenging regimes.
AI.conclusion: Presenting strong lensing images in polar representation is a computationally inexpensive way to improve CNN-based subhalo detection, especially where perturbations are hardest to detect.

title: Helical radio jets as probes of magnetised cluster environments: Periodic Faraday Rotation Revealed in the Corkscrew Galaxy by POSSUM
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) that exhibit regular plane-of-sky oscillations may provide a probe of magnetised plasma within the jets and their local intracluster medium (ICM). If such morphologies trace three-dimensional helices, path length differences between near and far sides of the flow might imprint quasi-periodic signatures in Faraday rotation. We present ASKAP Band 2 (1296-1440 MHz) polarimetric observations of a helical-tailed radio galaxy (the "Corkscrew Galaxy") from early science data from the POlarisation Sky Survey of the Universe's Magnetism (POSSUM), and test whether its quasi-periodic morphology produces signatures in Faraday rotation. We detect significant RM oscillations with a spatial period of (342 +/- 101) arcsec, consistent within the Rayleigh resolution limit with the jet's lateral deviations ((290 +/- 72) arcsec). Cross-correlation analysis reveals systematic variation along the jet: the eastern section shows alignment between jet deviation and RM, consistent with a jet-associated or sheath-like Faraday screen, while the western section exhibits a phase shift, indicating a transition in the dominant Faraday-rotating medium and possible contribution from the local ICM. These results demonstrate that quasi-periodic RM signatures can disentangle the dominant Faraday-rotating medium in AGN jets, and show that in some embedded radio galaxies the dominant RM contribution arises near the source rather than the cluster foreground. We also outline reliability criteria required to avoid false positive detections and inadequate sampling. Helical jet structures therefore show strong promise as probes of magnetised cluster environments, a capability that will expand in the SKA era.

AI.tldr: ASKAP observations of a helical-tailed radio galaxy (the "Corkscrew Galaxy") reveal quasi-periodic Faraday rotation measure (RM) oscillations spatially correlated with jet oscillations, demonstrating that helical jet structures can probe magnetised environments in AGN jets and the ICM, with the dominant RM contribution arising near the source rather than the cluster foreground.
AI.motivation: Jets from AGN that exhibit regular plane-of-sky oscillations may probe magnetised plasma within the jets and the local intracluster medium (ICM). If such morphologies trace 3D helices, path length differences between near and far sides of the flow might imprint quasi-periodic signatures in Faraday rotation.
AI.method: ASKAP Band 2 (1296-1440 MHz) polarimetric observations from POSSUM early science data were used to observe the "Corkscrew Galaxy." RM oscillations were detected and cross-correlation analysis was performed along the jet to examine the relationship between jet deviation and RM.
AI.result: Significant RM oscillations with a spatial period of 342±101 arcsec were detected, consistent with the jet's lateral deviations (290±72 arcsec). Cross-correlation showed eastern section alignment between jet deviation and RM (consistent with jet-associated or sheath-like Faraday screen), while western section exhibited a phase shift (indicating transition in the dominant Faraday-rotating medium and possible ICM contribution).
AI.conclusion: Quasi-periodic RM signatures can disentangle the dominant Faraday-rotating medium in AGN jets. In some embedded radio galaxies, the dominant RM contribution arises near the source rather than the cluster foreground. Helical jet structures show strong promise as probes of magnetised cluster environments, especially in the SKA era.

title: Probing Neutron Star Interiors and the Properties of Cold Ultra-dense Matter with the SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366) and arXiv:2512.16162
summary: Matter inside neutron stars is compressed to densities several times greater than nuclear saturation density, while maintaining low temperatures and large asymmetries between neutrons and protons. Neutron stars, therefore, provide a unique laboratory for testing physics in environments that cannot be recreated on Earth. To uncover the highly uncertain nature of cold, ultra-dense matter, discovering and monitoring pulsars is essential, and SKAO will play a crucial role in this endeavour. In this chapter, we will present the current state-of-the-art in dense matter physics and dense matter superfluidity, and discuss recent advances in measuring global neutron star properties (masses, moments of inertia, and maximum rotation frequencies) as well as non-global observables (pulsar glitches and free precession). We will specifically highlight how radio observations of isolated neutron stars and those in binaries -- such as those performed with SKAO in the near future -- inform our understanding of ultra-dense physics and address in detail how SKAO's telescopes unprecedented sensitivity, large-scale survey and sub-arraying capabilities will enable novel dense matter constraints. We will also address the potential impact of dark matter and modified gravity models on these constraints and emphasise the role of synergies between SKAO and other facilities, specifically X-ray telescopes and next-generation gravitational wave observatories.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews how SKAO observations of pulsars — both isolated and in binaries — will provide stringent constraints on the properties of ultra-dense neutron star matter, including superfluidity, glitches, free precession, and global parameters, while also exploring the potential impacts of dark matter and modified gravity, and emphasizing synergies with X-ray and gravitational wave observatories.
AI.motivation: Neutron stars offer a unique laboratory for studying cold, ultra-dense matter at several times nuclear saturation density, conditions impossible to recreate on Earth. Understanding the highly uncertain nature of this matter requires discovering and monitoring pulsars.
AI.method: The chapter reviews current state-of-the-art in dense matter physics and superfluidity, focusing on measuring global properties (masses, moments of inertia, maximum rotation frequencies) and non-global observables (pulsar glitches, free precession). It emphasizes SKAO's unprecedented sensitivity, large-scale survey capabilities, and sub-arraying to enable novel constraints.
AI.result: SKAO observations will provide novel constraints on ultra-dense matter through pulsar monitoring. The chapter also addresses potential impacts from dark matter and modified gravity models on these constraints.
AI.conclusion: SKAO, in synergy with X-ray telescopes and next-generation gravitational wave observatories, will play a crucial role in advancing our understanding of cold, ultra-dense neutron star matter.

title: The MIRI Early Obscured-AGN Wide Survey (MEOW): A Population of Hidden AGN at $z \gtrsim 5$ Revealed by JWST/MIRI Imaging
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present the MIRI Early Obscured-AGN Wide Survey (MEOW), a JWST/MIRI imaging survey designed to detect dust-obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) across cosmic time, with a particular focus on the high-redshift universe at $z \gtrsim 5$. MEOW observes the GOODS-N and GOODS-S fields with 43 pointings covering 95 arcmin$^2$ with the F1000W and F2100W filters, reaching depths of 0.5 and 3.6 $μ$Jy ($5σ$), respectively. Using spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling combining MEOW photometry with archival HST, JWST/NIRCam, and SCUBA-2 data, we identify a sample of 16 MIRI-selected AGN at $z = 4.5$--$7.2$ (12 spectroscopically confirmed), spanning bolometric luminosities of $L_{\rm bol} = 10^{44.6}$--$10^{46.4}$~erg~s$^{-1}$. Twelve of the 16 AGN are newly identified in this work, including at least five narrow-line AGN representing the obscured population to which broad-line spectroscopic searches are insensitive. Two broad-line AGN exhibit markedly different mid-infrared emission properties, consistent with one being a little red dot (LRD) and the other either a typical AGN or an LRD with unusually strong hot-dust emission. The MIRI-selected AGN bolometric luminosity function at $z = 4.5$--$6$ yields number densities comparable to those of broad-line AGN and LRDs, suggesting that obscured AGN contribute significantly to the total AGN census at these epochs. The narrow-line AGN reside in diverse host environments, with evidence for both circumnuclear and host-galaxy-scale obscuration, pointing to multiple physical mechanisms at work. These results establish JWST/MIRI imaging as an indispensable component of a multi-faceted approach to a complete census of early supermassive black hole growth.

AI.tldr: The MEOW survey uses JWST/MIRI imaging to identify 16 dust-obscured AGN at z=4.5–7.2 (12 spectroscopically confirmed), including 12 newly discovered sources and at least 5 narrow-line AGN invisible to broad-line searches. The study finds that obscured AGN contribute significantly to the total AGN population at these epochs and establishes MIRI imaging as key for a complete census of early supermassive black hole growth.
AI.motivation: To detect and characterize dust-obscured AGN at high redshift (z≳5), which are missed by broad-line spectroscopic surveys, in order to obtain a complete census of supermassive black hole growth in the early universe.
AI.method: JWST/MIRI imaging survey (MEOW) covering 95 arcmin² in GOODS-N and GOODS-S with F1000W and F2100W filters; SED modeling combining MEOW, HST, NIRCam, and SCUBA-2 photometry to identify and characterize MIRI-selected AGN at z=4.5–7.2.
AI.result: Identified 16 MIRI-selected AGN at z=4.5–7.2 (12 new, 12 spectroscopic confirmation); 5 narrow-line AGN (obscured population); two broad-line AGN with distinct mid-IR properties (one LRD, one atypical); bolometric LF suggests obscured AGN number densities comparable to broad-line AGN and LRDs at z=4.5–6.
AI.conclusion: Obscured AGN contribute significantly to the high-redshift AGN census; JWST/MIRI imaging is indispensable for a complete understanding of early supermassive black hole growth, revealing multiple obscuration mechanisms across diverse host environments.

title: A Shock-based Interpretation of Radio and X-ray Emission in Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: Accepted for publication in APJ. 15 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: We propose a shock-based framework to interpret the radio and X-ray emission in active galactic nuclei (AGNs), whose origin remains an open problem. In this framework, the radio emission is produced by synchrotron radiation in the accretion flow or a jet/weak outflow, while the dominant X-ray component depends on the accretion state, the location of the non-thermal emission region, and the available seed photon field. The model provides a self-consistent interpretation of radio and X-ray emission in typical non-jetted AGNs, including low-luminosity AGNs, Seyfert galaxies, and radio-quiet quasars. In jetted AGNs, our results disfavor scenarios in which the non-thermal electrons responsible for X-ray emission are accelerated in the disk or the corona. We use two widely discussed empirical diagnostics, radio loudness and the fundamental plane (FP) of black hole (BH) activity, to assess the applicability and limitations of the model. It can naturally explain the observed trends that the radio loudness increases with BH mass and decreases with the Eddington ratio. The observed slope of the FP depends on how the key physical quantities scale with the accretion rate. As the accretion rate increases, the advection-dominated accretion flow region contracts while the thin disk region expands, reflecting a transition toward a more radiatively efficient accretion structure. The Eddington ratio therefore influences the accretion structure, and may in turn shape the observed AGN classes.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a shock-based framework that self-consistently interprets radio and X-ray emission in AGNs, where radio comes from synchrotron radiation in the accretion flow or weak outflow, and the dominant X-ray component depends on accretion state and emission region location. The model explains observed trends in radio loudness and the fundamental plane of black hole activity, showing that accretion structure transitions from advection-dominated to thin disk as accretion rate increases, shaping AGN classes.
AI.motivation: The origin of radio and X-ray emission in AGNs remains an open problem, motivating the authors to develop a unified shock-based framework to self-consistently interpret these emissions across different AGN types.
AI.method: A shock-based theoretical framework is constructed where radio emission arises from synchrotron radiation in the accretion flow or jet/weak outflow, and the dominant X-ray component is determined by the accretion state, location of the non-thermal emission region, and available seed photon field. The model is tested against two empirical diagnostics: radio loudness and the fundamental plane of black hole activity.
AI.result: The model naturally explains that radio loudness increases with BH mass and decreases with Eddington ratio. The observed slope of the fundamental plane depends on how key physical quantities scale with accretion rate. For jetted AGNs, the results disfavor scenarios where non-thermal electrons for X-ray emission are accelerated in the disk or corona. As accretion rate increases, the advection-dominated accretion flow region contracts while the thin disk region expands.
AI.conclusion: The Eddington ratio influences the accretion structure, which in turn shapes observed AGN classes. The framework provides a self-consistent interpretation of radio and X-ray emission in typical non-jetted AGNs, including low-luminosity AGNs, Seyfert galaxies, and radio-quiet quasars.

title: Small-scale dynamo saturation across magnetic Prandtl numbers using the EDQNM closure
comment: 13 pages, 19 figures (excluding appendix). Comments are welcome
summary: Small-scale dynamos (SSDs) are believed to be the primary source of magnetic fields in all turbulent astrophysical systems, especially those with weak rotation such as elliptical galaxies and galaxy clusters. The initial kinematic phase of these dynamos is relatively well understood. Here we demonstrate analytically and numerically that, in an appropriate limit, the eddy-damped quasi-normal Markovian (EDQNM) closure for incompressible magnetohydrodynamic turbulence is strictly equivalent to the earlier models of kinematic dynamos. Moreover, it allows the extension of the kinematic dynamo framework to multi-scale turbulent flows and into the nonlinear regime. The EDQNM closure also enables us to explore a wide parameter range which is inaccessible to direct numerical simulations of the SSD. Using nonhelical EDQNM simulations, we identify several asymptotic regimes of nonlinear dynamo action when the system is highly turbulent with fluid Reynolds number $Re \gtrsim 10^6$ for magnetic Prandtl number $Pm > 1$ and magnetic Reynolds number $Rm \gtrsim 10^6$ for $Pm < 1$: 1) the kinematic growth rate approaches a value independent of $Pm$, 2) the saturated magnetic to kinetic energy ratio similarly converges to $\simeq 0.55$ across $Pm$, while the ratio of magnetic to kinetic integral wavenumbers asymptotes to $\simeq 3$. For all $Pm$, we further find strong feedback between magnetic field and velocity field largely via Alfvénisation leading to a saturated kinetic and magnetic spectra with almost the same inertial range with a slope of $-3/2$. These findings could provide guidance for future global simulations and for modeling the nonlinear regime of astrophysical systems living in these extreme limits.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the EDQNM closure for MHD turbulence is equivalent to kinematic dynamo models, extends it to multi-scale and nonlinear regimes, and identifies asymptotic dynamo regimes at extreme Reynolds numbers where growth rates become Pm-independent, saturated energy ratio converges to ~0.55, and spectra develop a -3/2 slope.
AI.motivation: Small-scale dynamos (SSDs) are believed to be the primary magnetic field source in weakly rotating turbulent astrophysical systems (elliptical galaxies, galaxy clusters). While the kinematic phase is understood, the nonlinear regime and extreme parameter ranges (high Re, Rm) remain inaccessible to direct numerical simulations.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate analytical equivalence between the EDQNM closure for incompressible MHD turbulence and earlier kinematic dynamo models. They perform nonhelical EDQNM simulations to explore parameter ranges inaccessible to DNS, covering various Pm and extreme Re/Rm regimes.
AI.result: Identified three asymptotic regimes: (1) kinematic growth rate becomes Pm-independent at Re≳10⁶ (Pm>1) or Rm≳10⁶ (Pm<1); (2) saturated magnetic-to-kinetic energy ratio converges to ~0.55; (3) spectral ratio of magnetic to kinetic integral wavenumbers asymptotes to ~3. Strong Alfvénisation feedback yields saturated kinetic/magnetic spectra with -3/2 slope across all Pm.
AI.conclusion: EDQNM closure provides a powerful tool to study SSD nonlinear regimes at astrophysically relevant extreme parameters. The asymptotic scaling laws and spectral slopes offer guidance for future global simulations and modeling of magnetic field amplification in systems like galaxy clusters.

title: High-Energy Neutrino Tomography of the Earth's Interior with IceCube
summary: The Earth's interior reflects its geological evolution, from accretion to present-day dynamics. Its structure drives the geodynamo in the outer core, generating the magnetic field that shields the surface from charged cosmic radiation. The primary observables of the Earth's interior are its radial density distribution and derived quantities such as its mass and moment of inertia. These have traditionally been inferred from gravity and seismic wave propagation, which probe the macroscopic response of matter to gravitational and elastic forces. Here we instead constrain the Earth's density profile using high-energy neutrinos observed by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole. We analyze 10.7 years of predominantly muon-neutrino data spanning 500 GeV--100 TeV, including atmospheric neutrinos produced by cosmic-ray interactions in the Earth's atmosphere and the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux. Neutrino attenuation depends on both the traversed column density and neutrino energy. By measuring the zenith- and energy-dependent flux suppression, we infer the Earth's radial density profile by fitting a concentric uniform-density shell model that incorporates neutrino fluxes, interaction cross sections, detector response, and glacial-ice systematic uncertainties. From the resulting density posteriors, we derive the Earth's mass and polar moment of inertia as measured by neutrinos. These are the most precise weak-interaction measurements of these quantities to date and are consistent with the Preliminary Reference Earth Model and independent gravitational determinations. Our results demonstrate that neutrinos provide a novel probe of planetary interiors via a distinct physical interaction, complementing gravity and seismology. With improved detectors and precision, neutrinos will further contribute to a multifaceted understanding of the Earth's structure.

AI.tldr: Using 10.7 years of IceCube neutrino data (500 GeV–100 TeV), the Earth's radial density profile is inferred from neutrino attenuation patterns, yielding mass and polar moment of inertia measurements consistent with the Preliminary Reference Earth Model. This demonstrates neutrinos as a novel, complementary probe of planetary interiors via weak interactions.
AI.motivation: Traditional inference of Earth's density structure relies on gravity and seismic wave propagation (elastic/gravitational forces). This work aims to provide an independent, complementary probe using high-energy neutrinos, which interact via the weak force and offer a distinct physical interaction mechanism to constrain planetary interiors.
AI.method: Analyze 10.7 years of IceCube muon-neutrino data (500 GeV–100 TeV), including atmospheric and diffuse astrophysical neutrinos. Measure zenith- and energy-dependent flux suppression caused by neutrino attenuation through the Earth. Fit a concentric uniform-density shell model incorporating neutrino fluxes, interaction cross sections, detector response, and glacial-ice systematic uncertainties to infer the radial density profile.
AI.result: Derived Earth's mass and polar moment of inertia from neutrino-based density posteriors, achieving the most precise weak-interaction measurements of these quantities. Results are consistent with the Preliminary Reference Earth Model and independent gravitational determinations.
AI.conclusion: Neutrinos provide a novel, complementary probe of planetary interiors via weak interactions, distinct from gravity and seismology. With improved detectors and precision, neutrinos will contribute further to a multifaceted understanding of Earth's structure.

title: Satellite quenching by radio jets of central galaxies in galaxy groups
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures (7 supplementary figures), submitted
summary: Feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) is now recognized as a key component of galaxy formation models. It plays a central role in regulating the growth and quenching of galaxies in the center of groups. However, the impact of AGN feedback from central galaxies on satellite galaxies remains largely unexplored. Here based on the largest sample to date of radio AGNs in galaxy groups (Yang et al. 2007) and a comprehensive consideration of multiple physical parameters that may influence the star formation of satellite galaxies, we demonstrate that the quiescent satellite fraction around radio AGNs is higher than that around normal galaxies. The most significant enhancement is observed around AGNs with large radio lobes. These findings demonstrate that the impact of kinetic AGN feedback beyond their host galaxies to their satellites. These results provide novel insights into the physical origins of some long-standing puzzles in extragalactic astronomy, including, e.g., galactic conformity and the strong small-scale clustering of quiescent galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using the largest sample of radio AGNs in galaxy groups, this study shows that satellite galaxies around radio AGNs (especially those with large radio lobes) are more likely to be quiescent than those around normal galaxies, demonstrating that kinetic AGN feedback extends beyond host galaxies to affect satellites.
AI.motivation: While AGN feedback is known to regulate central galaxy growth and quenching, its impact on satellite galaxies in groups remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: Analysis of the largest sample to date of radio AGNs in galaxy groups (Yang et al. 2007), with comprehensive consideration of multiple physical parameters influencing satellite star formation.
AI.result: The quiescent satellite fraction is higher around radio AGNs than around normal galaxies, with the most significant enhancement around AGNs with large radio lobes.
AI.conclusion: Kinetic AGN feedback impacts satellites beyond the host galaxy, providing insights into galactic conformity and the strong small-scale clustering of quiescent galaxies.

title: Non-thermal emission in jets and winds: Expected emission and spectral index distributions
comment: Submitted to MNRAS. 23 pages, 13 figures
summary: The origin of synchrotron emission in compact radio sources associated with active galactic nuclei (AGN) remains poorly understood. In a series of papers, we have examined diagnostic tools to disentangle the dominant underlying processes. In this study, we investigate the in situ evolution of cosmic-ray electrons (CREs) in compact AGN jets and winds, and examine how their evolution shapes the resulting observable radio properties. In jets, CREs experience multiple shock interactions as they propagate along the spine toward the hotspot and flow into the cocoon via backflows. In winds, CREs are predominantly accelerated at the Mach disc, with occasional re-acceleration within turbulent cocoon backflows. The continuous mixing of different CRE populations within the cocoon produces observational signatures that cannot be inferred from instantaneous conditions alone. In all jet simulations, spectral indices are flattest near the hotspot and steepen progressively away from the hotspots. In winds, spectra steepen with increasing distance from the Mach disc, with this trend becoming more pronounced at high radio frequencies due to radiative losses. We find the Mach disc to be a significantly more efficient CRE acceleration site than the forward shock in winds, which weakens as the wind expands to large scales. Since morphology, especially at low resolution, can be ambiguous for compact sources, spatially resolved spectral indices, particularly when combined with emission and polarization signatures, can provide a powerful diagnostic.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how cosmic-ray electrons evolve in compact AGN jets and winds, finding that spectral indices flatten near hotspots (jets) or Mach discs (winds) and steepen with distance, with the Mach disc being a more efficient acceleration site than forward shocks.
AI.motivation: The origin of synchrotron emission in compact radio sources associated with AGN remains poorly understood, motivating the need for diagnostic tools to disentangle the dominant underlying processes.
AI.method: The study uses simulations to trace the in situ evolution of cosmic-ray electrons (CREs) in compact AGN jets and winds, examining shock interactions, propagation along jet spines, backflows into cocoons, and acceleration at Mach discs versus forward shocks.
AI.result: In jets, spectral indices are flattest near hotspots and progressively steepen away from them. In winds, spectra steepen with distance from the Mach disc, especially at high radio frequencies due to radiative losses. The Mach disc is a significantly more efficient CRE acceleration site than the forward shock.
AI.conclusion: Spatially resolved spectral indices, combined with emission and polarization signatures, serve as powerful diagnostic tools for compact AGN sources, where morphology alone at low resolution can be ambiguous.

title: Direct Evidence for Outflow Driven by Wolf-Rayet Stars in the Nearby Galaxy PGC44685
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures, Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Wolf--Rayet (WR) stars are evolved massive stars which can drive strong stellar winds, injecting energy and momentum into the interstellar medium (ISM). However, the geometry and kinematics of WR-dominated outflows, specially in low-metallicity environments, is still poorly constrained by observations. We present a spatially resolved spectroscopic study of a WR region in a nearby dwarf galaxy, PGC\,44685, using high-resolution MEGARA IFU data from the Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC). After decomposing the [\textsc{O iii}]~$\lambda5007$ emission line with narrow and broad components, we verify a WR-driven outflow with a velocity reaching up to $20\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ relative to the systemic velocity. By use of the velocity and flux of the [\textsc{O iii}] broad component, we estimate an outflow mass of $(8.25 \pm 3.03)\times10^{3}\,M_\odot$ and a mass-loss rate of $(9.47 \pm 3.48)\times10^{-4}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. The corresponding kinetic power and momentum injection rate are $(4.77 \pm 1.77)\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ and $(8.20 \pm 3.02)\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-2}}$, respectively. The inferred low energy-loading efficiency ($\sim0.35\%$), together with the low metallicity of the WR region ($\sim0.1\,Z_\odot$), suggests that the system is observed in an early feedback phase in which stellar winds have not yet efficiently coupled their energy into the ISM. These results support the ability of WR feedback to shape the ISM on sub-kiloparsec scales, while these winds fail to launch galactic-scale outflows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a spatially resolved spectroscopic study of a Wolf-Rayet region in the dwarf galaxy PGC 44685 using GTC/MEGARA IFU data. By decomposing the [O III] λ5007 emission line, the authors identify a WR-driven outflow with velocities up to 20 km/s, estimate outflow mass of ~8.25×10³ M⊙ and mass-loss rate of ~9.47×10⁻⁴ M⊙ yr⁻¹, and find low energy-loading efficiency (~0.35%) in a low-metallicity (~0.1 Z⊙) environment, suggesting an early feedback phase where stellar winds have not yet efficiently coupled energy into the ISM.
AI.motivation: The geometry and kinematics of WR-dominated outflows, especially in low-metallicity environments, remain poorly constrained observationally. This study aims to address this gap by investigating a WR region in a nearby dwarf galaxy.
AI.method: Spatially resolved spectroscopic study using high-resolution MEGARA IFU data from the Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC). Decomposition of the [O III] λ5007 emission line into narrow and broad components to trace the outflow.
AI.result: WR-driven outflow with velocities up to 20 km/s; outflow mass of (8.25 ± 3.03)×10³ M⊙; mass-loss rate of (9.47 ± 3.48)×10⁻⁴ M⊙ yr⁻¹; kinetic power of (4.77 ± 1.77)×10⁴¹ erg s⁻¹; momentum injection rate of (8.20 ± 3.02)×10²⁸ g cm s⁻²; low energy-loading efficiency (~0.35%); low metallicity (~0.1 Z⊙).
AI.conclusion: The system is observed in an early feedback phase where stellar winds have not yet efficiently coupled energy into the ISM. WR feedback can shape the ISM on sub-kiloparsec scales but fails to launch galactic-scale outflows.

title: Evidence for Asymmetric Ejecta and Circumstellar Material in SN 2023ixf Inferred from Extensive Nebular-phase Observations
comment: 36 pages, 15 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: We present extensive optical and near-infrared (NIR) observations of the nearby Type II supernova (SN II) 2023ixf in the nebular phase from +89 days to +749 days after explosion, supplemented with NIR and mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope. The H$α$ emission profile shows complex evolution, with the emergence of high-velocity components consistent with the outer ejecta interacting with extended, low-density circumstellar material (CSM). We find that the H$α$ profile at an intermediate epoch (around +375 d) can be reconstructed by scaling an earlier decay-powered component and a later-phase shock-powered component, which revealed an additional intermediate-width component. This is consistent with the ejecta crashing into the initially aspherical dense CSM that has been swept-up by the forward shock. In the NIR, we find double-peaked emission from Mg I $1.504\ {\rm μm}$, Na I $2.206\ {\rm μm}$, and [Ni I] $3.12\ {\rm μm}$ between +200 d and +374 d, consistent with an asymmetric distribution of Ni-rich material that heats the ejecta inhomogeneously. We posit a disk-like CSM geometry and an ejecta geometry in which at least two large Ni-rich plumes lead to the observed line-profile diversity.

AI.tldr: SN 2023ixf shows complex nebular-phase emission from +89 to +749 days, with Hα profiles revealing ejecta-CSM interaction and double-peaked NIR/MIR lines indicating asymmetric Ni-rich ejecta plumes, consistent with a disk-like CSM geometry.
AI.motivation: To understand the late-phase evolution and asymmetric structure of SN 2023ixf through detailed nebular spectroscopy, revealing the interplay between the supernova ejecta and its circumstellar environment.
AI.method: Optical/NIR/MIR observations from +89 to +749 days, including JWST spectroscopy; Hα profile decomposition into decay-powered and shock-powered components; analysis of double-peaked NIR lines (Mg I, Na I, [Ni I]).
AI.result: Hα evolution shows high-velocity components from ejecta-CSM interaction; intermediate-epoch profile reconstructed by scaling two components; double-peaked NIR lines indicate asymmetric Ni-rich ejecta heating.
AI.conclusion: The data support a disk-like CSM geometry with aspherical, Ni-rich ejecta plumes producing the observed line-profile diversity.

title: Revisiting the Radial Velocities of Nearby Open Clusters using Gaia DR3
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in PASP
summary: Open clusters (OCs) are essential laboratories for probing stellar dynamics and tracing the structure and evolution of the Milky Way. Accurate measurements of their average radial velocities (RVs) and RV dispersions are crucial for estimating dynamical masses, orbital evolution, and overall kinematic states. Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) provides an unprecedented volume of high-precision RVs. However, when applied to OCs, Gaia DR3 RVs often yield unusually large and overestimated RV dispersions. This inflation is primarily driven by RV measurement systematics for hot and faint stars, as well as unresolved binary contamination. To mitigate this, we revisit the average RVs and RV dispersions of OCs within 500 pc of the Sun using Gaia DR3. We evaluate the reliability of RV measurements and employ a color-based filtering method. By selecting member stars within an intrinsic color range of $0.2 \le (BP-RP)_{0} \le 1.2$ mag, we exclude hot and cool stars with less reliable RVs. This filtering significantly reduces the inferred RV dispersions while maintaining average RVs consistent with previous literature. Specifically, the median RV dispersion decreases by 26%, dropping from 3.76 km s$^{-1}$ prior to filtering to 2.79 km s$^{-1}$ afterward. These filtered RV dispersions remain systematically larger than tangential velocity dispersions, likely due to residual biases and undetected binaries. However, RV dispersions measured exclusively from red clump giants (found in 6 clusters) are remarkably small ($\lesssim 1.6$ km s$^{-1}$) and align closely with tangential dispersions ($\lesssim 1$ km s$^{-1}$). Ultimately, we provide a practical, Gaia-only strategy to derive more realistic RV dispersions for OCs, identifying red clump giants as exceptionally high-fidelity kinematic tracers for robust cluster studies.

AI.tldr: Gaia DR3 RVs for open clusters near the Sun (<500 pc) suffer from inflated RV dispersions due to measurement systematics in hot/faint stars and binary contamination. A color-based filter ($0.2 \le (BP-RP)_0 \le 1.2$ mag) reduces median RV dispersion by 26% (from 3.76 to 2.79 km/s). Red clump giants yield the most reliable dispersions ($\lesssim 1.6$ km/s), closely matching tangential dispersions, and are identified as optimal kinematic tracers.
AI.motivation: Accurate average RVs and RV dispersions of open clusters are needed for dynamical mass estimation and kinematic studies, but Gaia DR3 RVs produce overestimated dispersions due to systematics in hot/faint stars and unresolved binaries.
AI.method: Reliability evaluation of Gaia DR3 RVs; color-based filtering selecting member stars within $0.2 \le (BP-RP)_0 \le 1.2$ mag to exclude problematic hot and cool stars; comparison with red clump giants as high-fidelity tracers.
AI.result: Median RV dispersion decreased by 26% from 3.76 to 2.79 km/s after filtering; filtered dispersions still larger than tangential dispersions; red clump giants (6 clusters) yield dispersions $\lesssim 1.6$ km/s, closely matching tangential values ($\lesssim 1$ km/s).
AI.conclusion: A practical Gaia-only strategy using color filtering and red clump giants provides more realistic RV dispersions for open clusters, identifying red clump giants as exceptionally high-fidelity kinematic tracers.

title: No Strong Evidence for Plasma Lensing in FRB 20240114A
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures; submitted for publication
summary: FRB~20240114A is an extremely active repeating fast radio burst for which plasma lensing has been proposed to explain its burst-rate variations, spectral evolution, and apparently ``carbon-copy'' burst pairs. Using FAST data and publicly available Parkes observations, we test this interpretation with a one-dimensional Gaussian plasma-lens model. Although the burst-rate enhancements can be fitted separately, the corresponding magnification peaks and demagnification troughs are offset by far more than predicted and show no consistent periodicity. Moreover, with more than 10,000 bursts detected, a few apparently ``carbon-copy'' pairs can readily occur by chance. The burst bandwidth is not systematically narrower during the proposed lensing interval, nor are the burst energies significantly enhanced during the predicted magnification interval. These results provide no compelling evidence that a single Gaussian plasma lens explains the observed variability, which is more likely dominated by intrinsic source activity.

AI.tldr: This paper tests the plasma-lensing interpretation for FRB 20240114A using FAST and Parkes data, finding no compelling evidence for a single Gaussian plasma lens; the observed variability is more likely intrinsic to the source.
AI.motivation: To test the proposed plasma-lensing explanation for the burst-rate variations, spectral evolution, and "carbon-copy" burst pairs observed in the extremely active repeating FRB 20240114A.
AI.method: The authors used FAST data and publicly available Parkes observations to test a one-dimensional Gaussian plasma-lens model against the observed properties of FRB 20240114A, examining burst-rate enhancements, magnification patterns, periodicity, occurrence of "carbon-copy" pairs, burst bandwidth, and burst energies.
AI.result: Burst-rate enhancements could be fitted separately, but magnification peaks and demagnification troughs were offset beyond predictions and lacked consistent periodicity. "Carbon-copy" pairs can occur by chance among >10,000 bursts. Burst bandwidth was not systematically narrower nor burst energies significantly enhanced during the proposed lensing interval.
AI.conclusion: No compelling evidence supports a single Gaussian plasma lens as the cause of the observed variability; the variability is more likely dominated by intrinsic source activity.

title: The Epoch of the GSE Merger: Insights from the Splash and Thick Disk Age Distributions
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letter
summary: The epoch of the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) merger, the last major merger experienced by the Milky Way, is crucial for reconstructing the Galaxy's evolutionary history. This event dynamically heated the disk, scattering some stars into the halo and producing the so-called Splash. Yet the observed age distribution of the Splash is systematically older than that of the thick disk from which it is thought to originate, posing a puzzling inconsistency. In this work, we show that this apparent discrepancy can be naturally explained once stellar age uncertainties are taken into account. The GSE truncated the intrinsic age distribution of the Splash at the merger epoch, while measurement errors introduce an Eddington-like bias that systematically shifts the truncated distribution toward older ages. Importantly, the magnitude of this shift depends on both the thick-disk star formation history and the merger epoch, thereby offering a new way to constrain the timing of the merger. By combining the observed Splash age distribution with the peak of thick-disk star formation, we infer a GSE merger epoch of $10.1^{+0.2}_{-0.2}$ Gyr ago, providing one of the tightest constraints to date. This result offers new insight into the Milky Way's accretion history and opens a path toward more robust reconstructions of its early evolution.

AI.tldr: The apparent age discrepancy between the Splash (older) and thick disk (younger) stars is explained by stellar age uncertainties causing an Eddington-like bias on the merger-truncated age distribution, yielding a GSE merger epoch of ~10.1 Gyr ago.
AI.motivation: Resolve the puzzling age discrepancy between the Splash population (systematically older) and the thick disk from which it originates, and constrain the timing of the last major merger (GSE) experienced by the Milky Way.
AI.method: Model the intrinsic age distribution truncated by the GSE merger, then incorporate stellar age measurement uncertainties to show that Eddington-like bias systematically shifts observed ages older; combine observed Splash age distribution with thick-disk star formation peak to infer merger epoch.
AI.result: The GSE merger epoch is constrained to 10.1^{+0.2}_{-0.2} Gyr ago, one of the tightest constraints to date. The age bias magnitude depends on both star formation history and merger epoch.
AI.conclusion: Stellar age uncertainties naturally explain the Splash-thick disk age discrepancy, and the merger epoch can be robustly inferred from this bias, offering new insight into Milky Way accretion history.

title: FAST Pulsar Database III. Snapshots of nulling, mode-changing and subpulse modulation of 374 pulsars
comment: 310 pages, 922 figures
summary: Based on sensitive L-band (1.0 to 1.5 GHz) observations of pulsars using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we analyzed single-pulse sequences from FAST-detected pulsars and identified nulling, mode changing, or subpulse modulation phenomena in 374 sources. Among these, nulling has been detected in 160 pulsars, with 127 cases reported for the first time. Emission mode changes have been observed in 52 pulsars, including 51 first-time detections. Subpulse modulation has been identified in 272 pulsars, 180 of which are newly revealed, with the majority displaying subpulse drifting behavior. Subpulse drifting in some pulsars exhibits distinct modes with varying drift properties, leading to mode changes and divergent mean profiles. Statistics on pulsar parameters show that pulsars exhibiting nulling and/or subpulse modulation tend to be older, with longer periods and lower spin-down energy-loss rates. The modulation period P3 is predominantly correlated with pulsar rotation periods, magnetic field strengths, and spin-down energy loss.

AI.tldr: Using FAST L-band observations of pulsars, the study analyzed single-pulse sequences from 374 sources, identifying nulling (160 pulsars, 127 new), emission mode changes (52 pulsars, 51 new), and subpulse modulation (272 pulsars, 180 new). Pulsars with these phenomena tend to be older with longer periods and lower spin-down energy loss. The modulation period P3 correlates with rotation period, magnetic field, and spin-down energy loss.
AI.motivation: To systematically identify and characterize nulling, mode changing, and subpulse modulation phenomena in a large sample of pulsars using the high sensitivity of FAST, and to reveal statistical relationships between these phenomena and fundamental pulsar parameters.
AI.method: Single-pulse sequences from FAST-detected pulsars were analyzed using sensitive L-band (1.0–1.5 GHz) observations. The analysis identified nulling, mode changing, and subpulse modulation across 374 sources, followed by statistical analysis of pulsar parameters.
AI.result: Nulling detected in 160 pulsars (127 new), emission mode changes in 52 pulsars (51 new), subpulse modulation in 272 pulsars (180 new, mostly subpulse drifting). Pulsars exhibiting nulling/subpulse modulation tend to be older, with longer periods and lower spin-down energy-loss rates. P3 correlates with rotation period, magnetic field strength, and spin-down energy loss.
AI.conclusion: FAST's sensitivity enables large-scale detection of single-pulse phenomena, revealing that nulling and subpulse modulation are common in older, slower-rotating pulsars. The correlations of P3 with fundamental parameters suggest underlying physical connections between emission modulation and pulsar magnetosphere properties.

title: Star Formation in the NE-Circinus Molecular Cloud Complex
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS. Data products (YSO catalogue, NEOWISE-R light curves) available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19904310
summary: This paper presents the first dedicated characterization of the NE-Circinus Complex (TGU H1984, DCld 320.7-03.6), a previously unstudied star-forming dark cloud complex serendipitously identified in archival Herschel SPIRE observations targeting the foreground Bok globules BHR 99 and BHR 100. Using Herschel SPIRE photometry, Planck Galactic Cold Clumps data, near-infrared 2MASS colour excess mapping, AllWISE photometry, Gaia DR3 photometry, and a 3D dust extinction map, the complex, and its embedded YSO population are characterized for the first time. Two independent photometric methods place the complex at 750 +/- 50 pc. Three morphologically distinct components are identified: a dense main cloud body, a diffuse eastern component, and a northern filamentary extension. The main cloud body has a SPIRE-derived dust temperature of 14.5 +/- 0.5 K. Near-infrared H-K colour excess mapping yields a core gas mass of ~277 Msun and a total gas mass of ~439 Msun, consistent with the Planck PGCC column density. An AllWISE YSO census identifies 39 candidates across all three components, confirming active star formation throughout the complex. Multi-epoch NEOWISE-R photometry reveals three significantly variable sources, including one aperiodic dipper - a previously uncatalogued YSO exhibiting dimming consistent with inner-disc occultation. Two previously uncatalogued compact Bok globules are identified on the western edge of the northern extension, both detected in SPIRE continuum emission. That this complex went uncharacterized despite Herschel data being publicly available since 2013 underscores the scientific value of archival examination and the incomplete state of southern sky molecular cloud inventories.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first characterization of the NE-Circinus Complex, a previously unstudied star-forming dark cloud at ~750 pc, identified serendipitously in archival Herschel data. Using multi-wavelength observations, it identifies three morphological components, a YSO population of 39 candidates, variable sources, and two new Bok globules, highlighting the value of archival data mining.
AI.motivation: To characterize the previously unstudied NE-Circinus Complex (TGU H1984, DCld 320.7-03.6), a star-forming dark cloud complex serendipitously discovered in archival Herschel SPIRE observations, and to demonstrate the scientific value of examining publicly available archival data for overlooked molecular cloud structures in the southern sky.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength analysis combining Herschel SPIRE photometry, Planck Galactic Cold Clumps data, near-infrared 2MASS colour excess mapping, AllWISE photometry, Gaia DR3 astrometry, and 3D dust extinction mapping. Two independent photometric methods for distance estimation. YSO identification via AllWISE colour diagnostics and variability analysis using multi-epoch NEOWISE-R photometry.
AI.result: Distance of 750 ± 50 pc; three morphological components (main cloud body at 14.5 ± 0.5 K, diffuse eastern component, northern filament); core gas mass ~277 M⊙, total gas mass ~439 M⊙; 39 YSO candidates identified; three significantly variable sources including an aperiodic dipper; two previously uncatalogued compact Bok globules detected.
AI.conclusion: The NE-Circinus Complex is an actively star-forming cloud that was overlooked despite publicly available Herschel data since 2013, underscoring the incomplete state of southern sky molecular cloud inventories and the importance of archival re-examination for discovering new star-forming regions.

title: Numerical Simulations of Restarted Jets -- I. Dynamics
comment: submitted to MNRAS
summary: We performed high-resolution three-dimensional relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations of restarted jets evolving within the cavity of a previous jet episode, using the PLUTO code. The simulations cover a spatial domain of $50\;\mbox{kpc}$ with a resolution of $40\;\mbox{pc}$. Three suites of simulations were performed to understand the impact of jet power, magnetic fields and quiescence time on the evolution of restarted jets. The restarted jets undergo a complex, multi-stage evolution, with the remnant cocoon relaxing from an initially conical structure to a mushroom-shaped morphology via an intermediate cylindrical phase. As the cocoon of the initial jet expands, dense material entrained by fluid instabilities such as Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Taylor significantly alter the conditions within it. As a result, the interaction of the restarted jet with the cocoon is markedly different from that of the initial jet with the ambient medium. In particular, we find that the restarted jet propagates ballistically through the rarefied remnant cocoon, without creating prominent backflows. Deceleration of the jet and associated backflows are observed only when it encounters dense structures. The structure and strength of the shocks in restarted jets are affected by jet power, magnetic field strength, and quiescence time. Finally, we discuss the implications of the dynamics for observed properties of radio galaxies.

AI.tldr: 3D RMHD simulations of restarted jets in radio galaxies show complex multi-stage evolution, with jets propagating ballistically through rarefied remnant cocoons and decelerating only upon encountering dense structures.
AI.motivation: To understand the complex dynamics of restarted jets in radio galaxies and how they evolve within the cavity of a previous jet episode, addressing the gap in knowledge about the interaction between successive jet outbursts.
AI.method: High-resolution (40 pc) 3D RMHD simulations using the PLUTO code over a 50 kpc domain, with three simulation suites varying jet power, magnetic field strength, and quiescence time between jet episodes.
AI.result: Restarted jets undergo multi-stage evolution (conical → cylindrical → mushroom-shaped cocoon morphology); they propagate ballistically through rarefied cocoons without prominent backflows; deceleration and backflows occur only at dense structures; shock structure/strength depend on jet power, magnetic field, and quiescence time.
AI.conclusion: The interaction of restarted jets with remnant cocoons differs significantly from initial jet-ambient medium interactions, with implications for observed radio galaxy properties.

title: Time Domain Studies of Active Galactic Nuclei with the SKA telescopes
comment: 13 pages. Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Bignall01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Time domain studies of active galactic nuclei (AGN) at radio wavelengths probe physical processes near the central engine via intrinsic variability, in particular within the relativistic jets, as well as small-scale structures in the local Galactic interstellar medium (ISM) via scintillation and scattering effects. Recent discoveries reinforce the expectation that the high sensitivity, large field-of-view, and broadband frequency coverage of the SKA telescopes will help to revolutionise our understanding of AGN populations and the evolution of jets, and allow detailed modelling of the structure and dynamics of scattering plasma in the local ISM over a large fraction of the sky.

AI.motivation: To understand physical processes near AGN central engines, relativistic jet evolution, and local ISM structures through radio time-domain variability.
AI.method: Time-domain radio observations using SKA's high sensitivity, large field-of-view, and broadband frequency coverage to analyze AGN variability and ISM scintillation/scattering.
AI.result: SKA will enable revolutionary understanding of AGN populations, jet evolution, and detailed modeling of ISM scattering plasma dynamics over large sky fractions.
