title: Galactic Centre Pulsars with the SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Abbate01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. An earlier version was published in The Open Journal of Astrophysics with arXiv ID: arXiv:2512.16155
summary: The detection of a pulsar closely orbiting our Galaxy's supermassive black hole - Sagittarius~A* - is one of the ultimate prizes in pulsar astrophysics. The relativistic effects expected in such a system could far exceed those currently observable in compact binaries such as double neutron stars and pulsar white dwarfs. In addition, pulsars offer the opportunity to study the magneto-ionic properties of Earth's nearest galactic nucleus in unprecedented detail. For these reasons, and more, a multitude of pulsar searches of the Galactic Centre have been undertaken, with the outcome of just seven pulsar detections within a projected distance of 100\,pc from Sagittarius~A*. It is currently understood that a larger underlying population likely exists, but it is not until observations with the SKA have started that this population can be revealed. In this chapter, we look at important updates since the publication of the last SKAO science book and offer a focused view of observing strategies and likely outcomes with the updated SKAO design.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews the status of pulsar searches near Sagittarius A*, noting only seven detections within 100 pc despite extensive efforts, and discusses how the SKA's updated design will enable discovery of the predicted larger pulsar population through new observing strategies.
AI.motivation: Detecting a pulsar orbiting Sagittarius A* is a major goal because such a system would exhibit extreme relativistic effects far beyond those seen in other compact binaries, and would allow detailed study of the magneto-ionic properties of the Galactic Centre.
AI.method: The chapter provides an update on pulsar search progress since the last SKAO science book, focusing on observing strategies and anticipated outcomes using the updated SKA design.
AI.result: Only seven pulsars have been detected within 100 pc of Sagittarius A* despite numerous searches, suggesting a larger hidden population exists that will require SKA observations to reveal.
AI.conclusion: The SKA, with its updated design and optimized observing strategies, is expected to uncover the long-sought pulsar population in the Galactic Centre, enabling transformative studies of relativistic gravity and the Galactic Centre environment.

title: Jet--ISM Interactions in Gaseous Disks: Simulating Kinetic Feedback in the Radio Galaxy 3C 326 N
comment: 21 pages, 21 figures, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Several radio galaxies, such as 3C\,326\,N, show signatures of jet--ISM coupling, but a complete theoretical framework for explaining them is still lacking. Interpreting these observations requires a detailed understanding of the gas distribution, geometry, and outflow energetics. In this paper, we use three-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamic simulations to investigate jet--ISM coupling in inhomogeneous gaseous disks, exploring a parameter space spanning different cloud configurations, jet powers, and central disk densities. Our simulations incorporate a numerical turbulence injection scheme that maintains vertical support in the disk, preventing the unphysical collapse encountered in previous studies. We find that jet--ISM coupling is strongly governed by the underlying cloud configuration, leading to distinct outflow morphologies, velocity dispersions, and kinetic energies. Simulations with small-scale ($l_{\rm c,max}=50$~pc) clouds produce the highest velocity dispersions and kinetic energies, whereas large-scale cloud configurations ($l_{\rm c,max}=250$~pc) yield the lowest values, with mixed cloud distributions exhibiting intermediate behavior. In addition, mixed cloud configurations give rise to asymmetric jet propagation, naturally producing unequal lobe lengths similar to those observed in radio galaxies. We compare our fiducial simulation (a $10^{45}\,\rm erg\,s^{-1}$ jet interacting with a mixed cloud configuration) with observations of 3C\,326\,N, focusing on the morphology of the jet-driven bubble, synthetic emission and the gas kinematics. Our results successfully reproduce the observed properties, providing strong evidence that jet--ISM interactions can account for the wide bubble and the complex gas kinematics observed in this system.

AI.tldr: Using 3D relativistic hydrodynamic simulations, this study shows that jet–ISM coupling in inhomogeneous disks is strongly governed by cloud configurations, with small-scale clouds producing the highest velocity dispersions and kinetic energies, and mixed cloud distributions yielding asymmetric jet propagation that successfully reproduces the observed features of 3C 326 N.
AI.motivation: Several radio galaxies show signatures of jet–ISM coupling, but a complete theoretical framework for explaining them is still lacking; interpreting observations requires detailed understanding of gas distribution, geometry, and outflow energetics.
AI.method: Three-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamic simulations of jet–ISM coupling in inhomogeneous gaseous disks, incorporating a numerical turbulence injection scheme that maintains vertical support and prevents unphysical collapse, exploring parameter space of cloud configurations, jet powers, and central disk densities.
AI.result: Small-scale clouds (l_c,max=50 pc) yield highest velocity dispersions and kinetic energies; large-scale clouds (l_c,max=250 pc) yield lowest values; mixed cloud distributions produce intermediate behavior and asymmetric jet propagation with unequal lobe lengths similar to observed radio galaxies. The fiducial simulation successfully reproduces observed morphology, synthetic emission, and gas kinematics of 3C 326 N.
AI.conclusion: Jet–ISM interactions can account for the wide bubble and complex gas kinematics observed in 3C 326 N, providing strong evidence that the proposed framework explains the observational signatures.

title: Understanding the Neutron Star Population with the SKAO Telescopes
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report number AASKAII/Levin01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. An earlier version of this chapter was published in The Open Journal of Astrophysics with arXiv ID: arXiv:2512.16156
summary: The known population of non-accreting neutron stars is ever growing and currently consists of more than 3500 sources. Pulsar surveys with the SKAO telescopes will greatly increase the known population, adding radio pulsars to every subgroup in the radio-loud neutron star family. These discoveries will not only add to the current understanding of neutron star physics by increasing the known sample, but will undoubtedly also uncover new types of sources that will challenge our theories of a wide range of physical phenomena. A broad variety of scientific studies will be made possible by a significantly increased population of neutron stars, unravelling questions such as: How do isolated pulsars evolve with time; What is the connection between magnetars, high B-field pulsars, and the newly discovered long-period pulsars; How is a pulsar's spin-down related to its radio emission; What is the nuclear equation of state? Increasing the numbers of pulsars in binary systems enables both larger numbers and higher precision tests of gravitational theories and general relativity, as well as probing the neutron star mass distribution. The excellent sensitivity of the SKAO telescopes combined with the wide field of view, large numbers of simultaneous tied-array beams that will be searched in real time, wide range of observing frequencies, and the ability to form multiple sub-arrays will make the SKAO an excellent facility for neutron star research. This chapter presents an overview of different types of neutron stars and discusses how the SKAO will aid in our understanding of the neutron star population.

AI.tldr: The SKAO telescopes will vastly increase the known population of non-accreting neutron stars (currently >3500 sources), enabling studies of pulsar evolution, magnetar connections, spin-down physics, the nuclear equation of state, and high-precision tests of gravity via binary systems.
AI.motivation: To leverage the SKAO's sensitivity, wide field of view, real-time tied-array beamforming, multi-frequency capabilities, and sub-array flexibility to greatly expand the known neutron star population and address fundamental questions about neutron star physics, evolution, and gravitational theories.
AI.method: Using SKAO telescopes to conduct pulsar surveys across multiple observing frequencies with real-time searching of numerous simultaneous tied-array beams, forming sub-arrays to optimize detection of diverse neutron star types.
AI.result: The SKAO will add radio pulsars to every subgroup of the radio-loud neutron star family, significantly increasing sample sizes and enabling discovery of new source types.
AI.conclusion: The SKAO will be an excellent facility for neutron star research, providing the population statistics and precision needed to probe pulsar evolution, emission mechanisms, the equation of state, and gravitational theories.

title: Kinetic temperature of massive star-forming molecular clumps measured with formaldehyde VI. The photodissociation region M17SW
summary: The kinetic temperature structure of the photodissociation region M17SW was mapped using the IRAM 30 m telescope. This mapping employed the para-H2CO triplet (J(KaKc) = 303-202, 322-221, and 321-220) near 218 GHz on a scale of ~0.2 pc. The kinetic temperatures were derived by modeling the average H2CO line ratios (322-221/303-202 + 321-220/303-202) with the RADEX non-local thermodynamic equilibrium approach. These temperatures range from 28 to 181 K with an average of 54.2 +/- 0.3 K at a spatial density of 5.5x10^5 cm^-3. Comparing with the temperature measurements obtained from multiple transitions of NH3 (1,1)-(6,6) and the far infrared (FIR) dust continuum, the H2CO lines show temperatures similar to those measured by NH3 but slightly higher than values derived from FIR observations. The high kinetic temperatures observed from H2CO are associated with the ultracompact H II region UC1, dense clumps, as well as H2O and CH3OH masers, showing a similar distribution as NH3. This indicates that dense gas in the M17SW region is heated by star formation activity. The presence of a significant gas temperature gradient across the M17SW region, as measured by H2CO and NH3, provides direct evidence for gas heated predominantly by radiation emitted from the OB star cluster NGC 6618. On a smaller scale, the dense gas surrounding the dense clumps experiences significant heating from internal protostars and/or young stellar objects. Higher temperatures traced by H2CO are linked to turbulence on a scale of ~0.2 pc. The complex temperature structure of the M17SW region is revealed by H2CO and NH3, which may be attributed to both large-scale external radiative heating and small-scale internal radiative and turbulent heating.

AI.tldr: The paper maps the kinetic temperature structure of the photodissociation region M17SW using H2CO line ratios observed with the IRAM 30 m telescope, finding temperatures from 28–181 K (avg. 54.2 K). Comparisons with NH3 and FIR dust show H2CO traces similar but slightly higher temperatures. Results reveal gas heating by the OB star cluster NGC 6618 on large scales and by internal protostars/YSOs on small scales, with turbulence contributing at ~0.2 pc scales.
AI.motivation: To map the kinetic temperature structure of the M17SW photodissociation region and understand the heating mechanisms (external radiative, internal protostellar, turbulent) affecting dense gas in star-forming regions.
AI.method: Mapping of para-H2CO triplet lines (303-202, 322-221, 321-220) near 218 GHz using IRAM 30 m telescope at ~0.2 pc resolution. Kinetic temperatures derived by modeling average H2CO line ratios with the RADEX non-LTE approach, assuming spatial density of 5.5×10^5 cm^-3. Comparison with NH3 (1,1)-(6,6) and FIR dust continuum temperature measurements.
AI.result: Kinetic temperatures range from 28 to 181 K, average 54.2±0.3 K. H2CO temperatures agree well with NH3 but are slightly higher than FIR dust values. High temperatures correlate with the ultracompact HII region UC1, dense clumps, H2O and CH3OH masers. A significant gas temperature gradient is observed across M17SW, with higher temperatures linked to turbulence at ~0.2 pc scale.
AI.conclusion: The dense gas in M17SW is heated predominantly by radiation from the OB star cluster NGC 6618 on large scales, while smaller-scale heating arises from internal protostars/YSOs and turbulence. H2CO and NH3 together reveal a complex temperature structure resulting from both large-scale external radiative heating and small-scale internal radiative and turbulent heating.

title: A Square Kilometre Array Pulsar Census
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Keane01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKA II) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. An earlier version of this chapter was published in The Open Journal of Astrophysics with arXiv ID: arXiv:2512.16153
summary: Most of the pulsar science case with the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) depends on long-term precision timing of a large number of pulsars, as well as their astrometric measurements using very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). However, before we can time them, or VLBI them, we must first find them. Here, we describe the considerations and strategies needed when planning an all-sky blind pulsar survey using the SKA. Based on our understanding of the pulsar population, the performance of the now-under-construction SKA elements, and practical constraints such as evading radio frequency interference, we project pulsar survey yields; this is done using two complementary methods for a number of illustrative survey designs, combining SKA-Low and SKA-Mid Bands 1 and 2 in a variety of ways. A composite survey using both SKA-Mid and SKA-Low is optimal, with Mid Band 2 focused in the plane. We find that, given its much higher effective area and survey speed, the best strategy is to use SKA-Low to cover as much sky as possible, ideally also overlapping with the areas covered by Mid. We find that an all-sky blind survey with Phase 1 of the SKA with the AA* array assembly will detect $\sim10,000$ slow pulsars and $\sim 800$ millisecond pulsars (MSPs) if SKA-Mid covers the region within $5°$ of the plane, while higher latitudes will be covered with SKA-Low. For the same survey region the yield with AA4 is $\sim 20\%$ higher, but this increases considerably by broadening the range covered by SKA-Mid Bands 1 and 2. In particular one could expect a yield of $\sim 1300$ MSPs with AA4. The pulsar census will enable us to set new constraints on the uncertain physical properties of the entire neutron star population. This will be crucial for addressing major SKA science questions including the dense-matter equation of state, strong-field gravity tests, and gravitational wave astronomy.

AI.tldr: This paper outlines strategies and projected yields for an all-sky blind pulsar survey using the SKA, combining SKA-Low and SKA-Mid (Bands 1 and 2). The optimal composite survey uses SKA-Low to cover as much sky as possible while SKA-Mid Band 2 focuses on the Galactic plane. Phase 1 with AA* is projected to detect ~10,000 slow pulsars and ~800 MSPs, while AA4 yields ~20% more, reaching ~1,300 MSPs. The resulting census will constrain neutron star physics and support SKA science goals like the dense-matter equation of state, tests of gravity, and gravitational wave astronomy.
AI.motivation: Most SKA pulsar science requires long-term precision timing of many pulsars and VLBI astrometry, but these pulsars must first be discovered via blind surveys. The paper aims to plan an optimal all-sky blind survey before the SKA can be used for timing and astrometry.
AI.method: The authors use two complementary population-model-based projection methods, consider SKA-Low and SKA-Mid (Bands 1 and 2) performance, practical constraints like RFI, and compare multiple survey designs combining different SKA elements and array assemblies (AA*, AA4).
AI.result: Phase 1 with AA* detects ~10,000 slow pulsars and ~800 MSPs if SKA-Mid covers |b|≤5° of the plane; AA4 yields ~20% more, with ~1,300 MSPs, especially if SKA-Mid Bands 1 and 2 coverage is broadened. SKA-Low should cover as much sky as possible, ideally overlapping with the Mid footprint.
AI.conclusion: A composite SKA-Low + SKA-Mid survey is optimal. The resulting pulsar census will enable new constraints on neutron star properties (dense-matter equation of state, strong-field gravity tests, gravitational wave astronomy), addressing major SKA science questions.

title: A steep mass transition for bar-driven ISM structuring revealed by PHANGS-JWST
comment: 17 pages, including the appendices, 10 Figures. Accepted for publication in the A&A Main Journal
summary: Galactic bars play a critical role in the secular evolution of their hosts by reorganising the ISM. We use a sample of 57 star-forming disc galaxies observed with JWST at 3 and 7.7 $μ$m to probe how the spatial distribution of PAH emission, as a structural marker of the cold ISM, depends on stellar mass and bar presence. We find evidence for a "watershed" at a stellar mass of $10^{10}$ Msun, marking a fundamental transition in the bar-driven distribution of PAH emission. This confirms trends previously predicted by numerical simulations and observed via ionised gas or UV light. While lower-mass galaxies exhibit a disordered and clumpy distribution of PAH emission regardless of bar presence, higher-mass barred hosts display well-structured dynamical features traced by PAH emission with significant gas reservoirs (e.g., discs and rings) within the central 15% of the bar radius (Rb). Furthermore, we observe a systematic depletion of PAH emission within the [0.2-0.8] Rb range in barred systems with stellar masses above $10^{10}$ Msun. Such central discs, rings, and associated radial dips ("bar deserts") appear to be a mass-dependent phenomenon: ubiquitous in massive galaxies but mostly absent in lower-mass counterparts. In contrast to the structured features in massive hosts, the disorganised ISM in lower-mass galaxies masks commonly observed bar-driven signatures. This suggests that tracer selection and dust obscuration may significantly bias observed bar fractions. Our study underlines two regimes of secular evolution, with different impacts and observability of bar-driven processes: it reaffirms bars as primary drivers of rapid secular evolution in galaxies above $10^{10}$ Msun$, while their impact is significantly reduced or delayed below this threshold. It further underscores the need to account for these processes when modelling galaxy evolution in cosmological simulations.

AI.tldr: Using JWST observations of 57 star-forming disc galaxies at 3 and 7.7 μm, this study finds a stellar mass threshold of 10¹⁰ M☉ that marks a fundamental transition in how galactic bars distribute PAH emission (a cold ISM tracer). Above this mass, barred galaxies show well-structured dynamical features (central discs, rings) and systematic PAH depletion in the [0.2–0.8] bar radius range ("bar deserts"), while lower-mass galaxies exhibit disordered, clumpy PAH distributions regardless of bar presence, indicating bar-driven secular evolution operates rapidly in massive galaxies but is reduced or delayed below this threshold.
AI.motivation: To understand how galactic bars reorganise the interstellar medium (ISM) and drive secular evolution across different stellar mass regimes, and to determine whether bar-driven signatures in the cold ISM are mass-dependent.
AI.method: Analysis of JWST observations at 3 and 7.7 μm for a sample of 57 star-forming disc galaxies, using PAH emission as a structural tracer of the cold ISM, and comparing barred versus unbarred systems across stellar mass.
AI.result: A stellar mass watershed at 10¹⁰ M☉ is identified. Higher-mass barred galaxies show well-structured PAH features (central discs and rings within 15% of bar radius) and systematic PAH depletion in the [0.2–0.8] Rb range ("bar deserts"). Lower-mass galaxies show disordered, clumpy PAH distributions irrespective of bar presence, masking bar-driven signatures.
AI.conclusion: Bar-driven secular evolution operates in two distinct regimes: rapid and observable in galaxies above 10¹⁰ M☉, but reduced or delayed below this threshold. Tracer selection and dust obscuration may bias observed bar fractions. Cosmological simulations must account for these mass-dependent processes.

title: Exploring the Magnetic Field Structure of the Milky Way with Pulsars in the SKA Era
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/JunXu01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. An earlier version of this chapter was published in The Open Journal of Astrophysics with arXiv ID: arXiv:2512.16159
summary: The magnetic field structure of the Milky Way can offer critical insights into the origin of galactic magnetic fields. Measurements of magnetic structures of the Milky Way are still sparse in far regions of the Galactic disk and halo. Pulsars are the best probes for the three-dimensional structure of the Galactic magnetic field, primarily owing to their highly polarized short-duration radio pulses, negligible intrinsic Faraday rotation compared to the contribution from the medium in front, and their widespread distribution throughout the Galaxy across the thin disk, spiral arms, and extended halo. In this article, we give an overview of Galactic magnetic field investigation using pulsars. The sensitive SKA1 design baseline (AA4) will increase the number of known pulsars by a factor of around three, and the initial staged delivery array (AA*) will probably double the total number of the current pulsar population. Polarization observations of pulsars with the AA* telescopes will give rotation measures along several thousand lines of sight, enabling detailed exploration of the magnetic structure of both the Galactic disk and the Galactic halo.

AI.tldr: Pulsars are excellent probes for mapping the Milky Way's 3D magnetic field structure due to their polarized signals and wide distribution. Future SKA1 observations will significantly increase known pulsars and rotation measure data, enabling detailed exploration of Galactic disk and halo magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin of galactic magnetic fields by mapping the magnetic field structure of the Milky Way, which remains poorly constrained in far regions of the disk and halo.
AI.method: Using pulsars as probes—leveraging their highly polarized short-duration radio pulses, negligible intrinsic Faraday rotation, and widespread distribution—to measure rotation measures along lines of sight. Future SKA1 telescopes (AA* and AA4) will multiply the known pulsar population and enable thousands of new rotation measure sightlines.
AI.result: SKA1 design baseline (AA4) will increase known pulsars ~3×; initial staged array (AA*) will roughly double the current pulsar population. Polarization observations with AA* will yield rotation measures along several thousand lines of sight.
AI.conclusion: The upcoming SKA1-era pulsar observations will enable detailed, three-dimensional exploration of both the Galactic disk and halo magnetic structures, significantly advancing our understanding of Galactic magnetism.

title: Advancing extragalactic spectral line studies with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/vanLoon01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: We present an overview of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) science potential in the area of extragalactic spectral lines besides 21-cm neutral hydrogen. It highlights the main points from the SKAO Science Book chapters on individual topics, but is augmented by additional prospects. The SKAO will push studies and use of masers, kilomasers, megamasers, molecular and radio-recombination-line emission and absorption to a wider variety of environments, including to very high redshift where it may detect the first molecule (HeH$^+$). It will open the door to measurements of hydrogen and helium isotopes, probing the conditions for star formation and Big Bang nucleosynthesis. While the planned SKAO of the 2030s (AA*) is destined to forge major progress, an SKAO as initially envisaged (AA4) will truly transform the landscape, and an extension towards higher frequencies (up to 24 GHz) would enable water maser and ammonia surveys in nearby galaxies and systematic molecular gas inventories at redshift 5.

AI.tldr: This paper overviews the SKAO's potential for studying extragalactic spectral lines (excluding 21-cm HI), including masers, molecules, and radio-recombination lines, from nearby environments to high redshift, with transformative prospects for detecting the first molecule (HeH$^+$), measuring hydrogen/helium isotopes, and conducting molecular gas surveys up to redshift 5.
AI.motivation: To present the SKAO's science potential for extragalactic spectral lines beyond 21-cm neutral hydrogen, highlighting key topics from the SKAO Science Book and additional prospects for studying masers, molecules, and isotopes across cosmic environments.
AI.method: Overview of SKAO capabilities for spectral line studies, including masers, kilomasers, megamasers, molecular lines, and radio-recombination lines in emission/absorption, with projections for high-redshift observations (HeH$^+$) and isotopic measurements (hydrogen, helium).
AI.result: SKAO will enable studies of spectral lines in diverse environments and at very high redshift, potentially detecting the first molecule HeH$^+$; the initially envisioned SKAO (AA4) will transform the field, and a higher-frequency extension (up to 24 GHz) would enable water maser and ammonia surveys in nearby galaxies and molecular gas inventories at z~5.
AI.conclusion: The SKAO holds transformative potential for extragalactic spectral line science, with the originally planned AA4 configuration being more impactful than the AA* baseline; extending to 24 GHz would further enable key surveys for water masers, ammonia, and molecular gas at high redshift.

title: Multiwavelength properties of short gamma ray bursts with extended emission observed by Swift
comment: Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: Short gamma-ray bursts with extended emission (SGRBEEs) are a particular class of long GRBs (LGRBs) which, despite their duration, share several observational features with short GRBs (SGRBs). They are composed by a short, hard initial pulse (IP) followed by a longer and softer extended emission (EE). We investigate whether SGRBEEs originate from the same progenitor as SGRBs despite their duration, representing a peculiar subclass of LGRBs, or if they constitute a distinct population. Given their respective duration, we tested if the IP and the EE share properties with short and long GRBs, respectively. We analysed SGRBEEs from the flux-limited, redshift-complete SBAT4 sample using prompt-emission data from Swift/BAT, Fermi/GBM and Konus-WIND, and X-ray afterglow observations from Swift/XRT. The temporal and spectral properties of the IP and EE components were compared with those of SGRBs from the extended SBAT4 sample and LGRBs from the BAT6 sample. Despite observing a clear spectral evolution during the prompt phase of each SGRBEE, IPs and EEs as well as short and long GRBs can not be distinguished by their hardness ratio only. All bursts analysed have a spectral lag consistent with zero. SGRBEEs XRT light curves are consistently more complex than those of SGRBs, requiring the addition of multiple breaks and showing the presence of steep decays and plateaus. Our results indicate that SGRBEEs are not an intermediate class. During prompt emission, despite common spectral features, IPs and EEs temporally differ from short and long GRBs, respectively. EEs are on average too faint to appear in the Amati plane, but IPs occupy the same parameter space of SGRBs. In the afterglow, SGRBEEs are more luminous than standard GRBs at early-time, suggesting a direct contribution from the EE; at later times, these events behave as standard SGRBs, and both remain systematically less luminous than LGRBs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether short gamma-ray bursts with extended emission (SGRBEEs) constitute a distinct population or are a subclass of short GRBs (SGRBs). Through analysis of prompt and afterglow emission from multiple instruments, the authors find that SGRBEEs are not an intermediate class: their initial pulses (IPs) resemble SGRBs temporally and spectrally, while extended emissions (EEs) differ from long GRBs. In afterglow, SGRBEEs show early-time EE contribution but later behave like standard SGRBs, remaining systematically less luminous than LGRBs.
AI.motivation: To determine whether SGRBEEs originate from the same progenitor as SGRBs (despite their longer duration) or constitute a distinct population, and to test if the IP and EE components share properties with short and long GRBs respectively.
AI.method: Analysis of SGRBEEs from the flux-limited, redshift-complete SBAT4 sample using prompt-emission data from Swift/BAT, Fermi/GBM, Konus-WIND, and X-ray afterglow observations from Swift/XRT. Temporal and spectral properties of IP and EE components were compared with SGRBs from the extended SBAT4 sample and LGRBs from the BAT6 sample.
AI.result: (1) IPs and EEs cannot be distinguished from SGRBs and LGRBs by hardness ratio alone; all bursts have spectral lag consistent with zero. (2) SGRBEE XRT light curves are more complex than SGRBs, with multiple breaks, steep decays, and plateaus. (3) EEs are too faint for the Amati plane; IPs occupy the same parameter space as SGRBs. (4) In afterglow, SGRBEEs are more luminous than standard GRBs at early times (EE contribution) but behave as standard SGRBs at later times, both less luminous than LGRBs.
AI.conclusion: SGRBEEs are not an intermediate class. IPs and EEs temporally differ from short and long GRBs respectively despite common spectral features. The results suggest SGRBEEs share progenitor origins with SGRBs rather than representing a distinct population.

title: Physically motivated AGN emissivity profiles and their effects on quasar microlensing signatures. 1. Multi-epoch accretion disc size inference
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 3 appendices. Submitted to A&A, comments welcome
summary: Quasar microlensing is uniquely sensitive to the size-scale of the accretion flow, offering one of the few direct probes of the accretion structure on micro-arcsecond scales. However, microlensing-based measurements in the optical and UV often find sizes systematically larger than expected from standard Shakura-Sunyaev disc theory, commonly referred to as the disc-size problem similar to that seen in continuum reverberation campaigns. But this assumes that all the emission comes from a single compact disc, neglecting the diffuse emission from the BLR which originates on much larger spatial scales. In this paper we directly quantify the effect of large-scale diffuse emission on the observed microlensing signatures. We adapt the physically motivated agnsed model to construct energetically self-consistent emissivity profiles in any given bandpass. Since this also predicts the full SED, we combine these SEDs with cloudy to give a diffuse BLR component. We convolve these models with representative microlensing magnification maps, and generate mock microlensing light curves to directly assess the inferred source size under different physical conditions. While the detailed shape of the disc emissivity profile has only a higher-order effect on the microlensing profile, the inclusion of the BLR makes a significant impact since this naturally smooths out the caustic network over larger scales. This introduces a significant bias when interpreted purely as a compact disc. However, the strength of this bias depends predominantly on the fractional contribution of the diffuse emission to the SED in the bandpass being considered, as this sets the effective half-light radius, giving an important wavelength dependence. We conclude that part of the excess in microlensing-inferred accretion disc sizes could arise from interpreting a composite (disc+BLR) picture as a single compact disc.

AI.tldr: Microlensing-inferred accretion disc sizes may appear too large because the diffuse emission from the Broad Line Region (BLR) is misinterpreted as part of a single compact disc, introducing a systematic bias that depends on the fractional BLR contribution to the observed bandpass.
AI.motivation: Quasar microlensing offers a direct probe of accretion structure on micro-arcsecond scales, but optical/UV measurements systematically yield larger disc sizes than predicted by standard Shakura-Sunyaev theory (the "disc-size problem"). The authors hypothesize that neglecting diffuse BLR emission, which originates on much larger scales, could explain this discrepancy.
AI.method: The authors adapt the agnsed model to construct energetically self-consistent emissivity profiles, combine these SEDs with cloudy to model diffuse BLR emission, convolve models with microlensing magnification maps, and generate mock light curves to assess inferred source sizes under different physical conditions.
AI.result: The disc emissivity profile shape has only a higher-order effect on microlensing, but including BLR emission significantly smooths the caustic network over larger scales, biasing size inferences when interpreted as a compact disc. The bias strength depends on the fractional BLR contribution to the SED in the observed bandpass, giving a characteristic wavelength dependence via the effective half-light radius.
AI.conclusion: Part of the excess in microlensing-inferred accretion disc sizes may stem from misinterpreting a composite (disc+BLR) emission structure as a single compact disc, rather than indicating a genuine failure of standard disc theory.

title: Beyond the Impulsive Approximation: The Dynamics and Radio Emission of Tidal Disruption Jets
comment: 11 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to ApJL. Comments welcome
summary: Radio emission from relativistic tidal disruption events (TDEs) is commonly interpreted using the Blandford--McKee solution for an impulsive relativistic blast wave. Unlike gamma-ray bursts, however, TDE jets are powered by fallback accretion, injecting energy over weeks to months. We investigate how this sustained energy injection modifies the dynamics and radio emission of relativistic TDE jets using one- and two-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamic simulations coupled with synchrotron radiation calculations. For a fixed total energy, fallback-powered jets drive slower forward shocks, producing delayed and systematically fainter radio emission. We show that the impulsive approximation is valid only when the duration of energy injection is less than approximately ten percent of the deceleration time of an equivalent Blandford--McKee blast wave, a condition that is generally not satisfied for relativistic TDEs. As a result, continuously powered outflows are significantly less beamed than impulsive explosions, leading to a strong suppression of off-axis radio emission. These results demonstrate that the radio evolution of relativistic TDEs retains memory of the central engine and cannot, in general, be described by an impulsive solution. By substantially reducing the expected off-axis radio emission, sustained fallback-powered jets imply that relativistic jet production in tidal disruption events may be considerably more common than current radio observations suggest.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that sustained energy injection from fallback accretion in relativistic TDE jets fundamentally alters their dynamics and radio emission compared to the impulsive Blandford-McKee solution, making them systematically fainter, less beamed, and poorly described by impulsive models. This implies relativistic TDE jets may be more common than radio observations indicate.
AI.motivation: Standard models of TDE radio emission use the impulsive Blandford-McKee blast wave solution, but TDE jets are powered by fallback accretion over weeks to months rather than impulsively. The authors investigate how this sustained energy injection modifies jet dynamics and radio emission.
AI.method: 1D and 2D relativistic hydrodynamic simulations coupled with synchrotron radiation calculations, comparing continuously powered jets to impulsive Blandford-McKee blast waves.
AI.result: Fallback-powered jets produce slower forward shocks, delayed and fainter radio emission. The impulsive approximation holds only when injection duration < ~10% of deceleration time (not satisfied for TDEs). Continuously powered outflows are significantly less beamed, strongly suppressing off-axis radio emission.
AI.conclusion: Radio evolution of relativistic TDEs retains memory of the central engine and cannot be described by impulsive solutions. Sustained jets imply relativistic jet production in TDEs may be considerably more common than current radio observations suggest.

title: PKS 2155-304: Long-Term Optical Photometric Monitoring and Variability Analysis
summary: Through the detailed study of the optical flux behaviour in blazars over time, it is possible to infer the conditions responsible for their observed emission. PKS 2155-304, a BL Lac object detected from radio to TeV energies, is among the brightest blazars in the southern hemisphere. We present optical monitoring spanning over two decades using telescopes at Complejo Astronómico El Leoncito and Estación Astrofísica de Bosque Alegre, Argentina. Differential light curves in the B, V, R, and I bands reveal significant variability on weekly and longer timescales, with occasional changes on sub-four-hour scales. The optical spectral index remained negative, consistent with non-thermal emission, and hardened over the past nine years. Evidence for quasiperiodic behaviour on 20-30 day timescales was found, while correlations with X-ray fluxes were weak, suggesting distinct emission components in the two bands. These results highlight the pronounced optical variability of PKS 2155-304 and provide insight into its multi-band emission mechanisms

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes over two decades of optical monitoring of the blazar PKS 2155-304, revealing significant variability on weekly to sub-four-hour timescales, a hardening optical spectral index over nine years, weak correlations with X-ray emissions, and evidence of quasiperiodic behavior on 20-30 day timescales.
AI.motivation: To infer the physical conditions responsible for the observed emission in blazars by conducting a detailed long-term study of the optical flux behavior of PKS 2155-304.
AI.method: Differential photometry in B, V, R, and I bands was performed using telescopes at Complejo Astronómico El Leoncito and Estación Astrofísica de Bosque Alegre, Argentina, over more than two decades of monitoring.
AI.result: Significant variability was detected on weekly and longer timescales, with occasional sub-four-hour changes. The optical spectral index remained negative (consistent with non-thermal emission) and hardened over the past nine years. Quasiperiodic behavior on 20-30 day timescales was found, while X-ray correlations were weak.
AI.conclusion: The pronounced optical variability of PKS 2155-304 and the weak optical-X-ray correlations suggest distinct emission components in the two bands, providing insight into the multi-band emission mechanisms of this blazar.

title: Neutrinos from super-Eddington Seyfert galaxies
comment: Under review for minor corrections in Astroparticle Physics
summary: Multimessenger observations suggest that Seyfert galaxies are promising sources of high-energy neutrinos, but their dense inner environments can strongly suppress the emerging very-high-energy gamma-ray emission. Active galactic nuclei (AGN) undergoing intense accretion episodes can enter a super-Eddington state, in which the accretion flow becomes geometrically and optically thick within a critical radius and develops strong magnetic fields in its innermost region. At the same time, large amounts of matter are expelled from the disk surface in the form of powerful, radiation-driven winds. In this work, we explore a scenario in which the cores of super-Eddington AGN provide suitable conditions for the acceleration of relativistic particles, including hadrons, via magnetic reconnection in a magnetically confined region close to the supermassive black hole. The accelerated hadronic component interacts with the intense photon field of the disk, leading to a copious neutrino flux peaking at 10-100 TeV that may be detectable with current observatories such as IceCube and KM3NeT, while the surrounding outflow efficiently absorbs the accompanying gamma-ray emission from the inner core. We also apply the model to the nearby super-Eddington Seyfert 1 NGC 7469 as a representative case with two reported neutrino events. In this framework, super-Eddington AGN, in particular Seyfert galaxies undergoing transient intense accretion episodes, emerge as plausible hidden neutrino sources, offering a natural explanation for the coexistence of efficient neutrino production and a strongly attenuated gamma-ray counterpart.

AI.tldr: Super-Eddington AGN, particularly Seyfert galaxies in intense accretion episodes, can produce detectable high-energy neutrinos (10-100 TeV) via hadronic acceleration through magnetic reconnection near the black hole, while their dense outflows absorb accompanying gamma rays, explaining hidden neutrino sources as exemplified by NGC 7469.
AI.motivation: Multimessenger observations suggest Seyfert galaxies are promising neutrino sources, but their dense environments suppress very-high-energy gamma rays. The paper seeks to explain the coexistence of efficient neutrino production and attenuated gamma-ray emission from AGN cores.
AI.method: The paper models a scenario where super-Eddington AGN cores accelerate relativistic particles (including hadrons) via magnetic reconnection in a magnetically confined region near the supermassive black hole. The accelerated hadrons interact with the intense disk photon field to produce neutrinos, while the surrounding outflow absorbs the accompanying gamma rays. The model is applied to NGC 7469 as a representative case.
AI.result: The model predicts a copious neutrino flux peaking at 10-100 TeV that may be detectable with IceCube and KM3NeT, with the outflow efficiently absorbing the gamma-ray counterpart.
AI.conclusion: Super-Eddington AGN, especially Seyfert galaxies undergoing transient intense accretion episodes, are plausible hidden neutrino sources, naturally explaining efficient neutrino production with a strongly attenuated gamma-ray counterpart.

title: Euclid: A UV-faint quasar in a highly luminous star-forming host galaxy at $z \approx 7.7$
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 1 table, Accepted for Publication in A&A
summary: Constraining the co-evolution of supermassive black holes and their host galaxies in the first billion years after the Big Bang is essential for understanding the formation of the earliest cosmic structures. Here, we present IRAM/NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) observations of the $z \approx 7.7$ quasar EUCL\,J125308.55+705432.3, recently discovered in the first data release of the Euclid Wide Survey. We report the most distant detections of [CII] 158$μ\mathrm{m}$ and cold dust emission in a quasar host to date. The [CII] emission line sets the systemic redshift at $z=7.6980\pm0.0004$. The source exhibits luminosities of $L_{\rm FIR}=3.6\times10^{12}\,L_{\odot}$ and $L_{[CII]}=2\times10^9\,L_{\odot}$, respectively, a dust mass of 1.4$\times 10^{8}\,M_{\odot}$, and a dynamical mass in the range 0.33-1.3$\times10^{10}\,M_{\odot}$. Remarkably, despite being nearly two magnitudes fainter in the rest-frame UV ($M_{1450}=-24.06$) than previously known $z\approx7.5$ quasars (<M$_{1450}$> $\sim-$26.5), EUCL\,J125308.55+705432.3 exhibits the brightest [CII] emission among them. This indicates that the host galaxy is actively star-forming, with a star-formation rate $>250\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, consistent with recent findings that UV-faint quasars at $z>6$ preferentially reside in [CII]-luminous galaxies. The UV-faintness likely reflects dust obscuration or sub-Eddington accretion, rather than lower host mass, suggesting these systems are at a different stage in their evolution compared to UV-bright quasars. These IRAM/NOEMA observations highlight the power of combining Euclid's wide-area quasar discovery potential with submillimetre follow-up observations to characterise the host galaxies of early supermassive black holes across a broader redshift and luminosity range than previously accessible.

AI.tldr: IRAM/NOEMA observations of the z≈7.7 quasar EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 reveal the most distant detections of [CII] 158μm and cold dust emission in a quasar host. The UV-faint quasar (M1450=-24.06) exhibits the brightest [CII] emission among known z≈7.5 quasars, indicating active star formation (SFR>250 M⊙/yr) and suggesting that UV-faintness stems from dust obscuration or sub-Eddington accretion rather than lower host mass.
AI.motivation: To constrain the co-evolution of supermassive black holes and their host galaxies in the first billion years after the Big Bang by studying a newly discovered UV-faint quasar at z≈7.7.
AI.method: IRAM/NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) submillimetre follow-up observations of the z≈7.7 quasar EUCL J125308.55+705432.3, identified in the Euclid Wide Survey first data release, targeting [CII] 158μm and cold dust emission.
AI.result: Detected [CII] and cold dust emission at z=7.6980±0.0004 — the most distant such detections in a quasar host. L_FIR=3.6×10^12 L⊙, L_[CII]=2×10^9 L⊙, dust mass=1.4×10^8 M⊙, dynamical mass=0.33-1.3×10^10 M⊙, SFR>250 M⊙/yr. Combining Euclid's wide-area surveys with submillimetre follow-up enables characterization of early SMBH hosts across a broader redshift and luminosity range.

title: Different dissipation mechanisms of jet underlying variability in blazars
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures
summary: Blazars are among the most extreme classes of active galactic nuclei. They are powered by relativistic jets, but the way in which the jet energy is dissipated is still unclear. The flat radio spectrum and the core-shift effect trace the distributions of magnetic fields and relativistic particles along the jet, while variability carries information about time-dependent dissipation. However, a unified framework connecting these observables to the underlying jet physics has been lacking. Here we present a multi-frequency analysis of the prototypical blazar Mrk~501. We model its core-shift measurements, spectral energy distributions (SEDs), and power spectral densities (PSDs) with a conical jet model that conserves magnetic power. The core-shift data localize the radio emitting regions and constrain the electron-density and dissipation-rate profiles along the jet. With a single radial distribution of jet parameters, the model reproduces the core-shift relation and SED, but it underpredicts the observed variability at high radio frequencies and in the optical to $γ$-ray bands. We therefore introduce different blob distributions for the inner ($\lesssim$~0.1\,pc) and outer ($\gtrsim$~0.1\,pc) jet regions. With this extended model, the simulated PSDs are consistent with the multiwavelength observations of Mrk~501 during its 2017--2019 low state. This result points to different dissipation behavior in the inner and outer jet. Our study demonstrates that spectro--timing--astrometric jet modeling, which combines SEDs, multiwavelength PSDs, and radio core-shift measurements, can constrain jet stratification and scale-dependent dissipation in blazars.

AI.tldr: The authors present a multi-frequency analysis of blazar Mrk~501 using a conical jet model that conserves magnetic power. They combine core-shift measurements, SEDs, and PSDs to constrain jet physics. A single radial distribution fails to reproduce observed variability, so they introduce separate blob distributions for inner (≲0.1 pc) and outer (≳0.1 pc) jet regions. The extended model successfully reproduces multiwavelength observations during the 2017–2019 low state, indicating different dissipation behavior in the inner vs. outer jet.
AI.motivation: A unified framework connecting core-shift measurements, spectral energy distributions, and variability to the underlying jet physics in blazars has been lacking.
AI.method: Multi-frequency analysis of Mrk~501 using a conical jet model with conserved magnetic power, combining radio core-shift measurements, SEDs, and PSDs. The model includes different blob distributions for the inner (≲0.1 pc) and outer (≳0.1 pc) jet regions.
AI.result: A single radial distribution reproduces the core-shift relation and SED but underpredicts variability at high radio frequencies and optical to γ-ray bands. The extended two-zone model produces PSDs consistent with multiwavelength observations of Mrk~501 during its 2017–2019 low state.
AI.conclusion: Spectro–timing–astrometric jet modeling (combining SEDs, multiwavelength PSDs, and radio core-shift measurements) can constrain jet stratification and scale-dependent dissipation in blazars, pointing to different dissipation behavior in the inner and outer jet.

title: Euclid: Discovery of 31 new quasars at $6.6 < z < 7.8$
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We report the discovery of 31 new high-$z$ quasars in the redshift range $6.6 < z < 7.8$. These quasars were selected from approximately 3000 deg$^2$ of sky covered during the first 1.5 years of the Euclid Wide Survey, representing the initial results of the Euclid high-$z$ quasar search. Our candidate selection employed multiple machine-learning and probabilistic techniques applied to the Euclid $I_E$, $Y_E$, $J_E$, and $H_E$ images, supplemented by ancillary $z$-band data when available. Spectroscopic follow-up observations were carried out with Keck, Magellan, and the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT). Among the new discoveries, there are 12 quasars at $z \geq 7$, more than doubling the number of previously known quasars at $z \geq 7$. The newly discovered quasars exhibit $21.2 < J_E < 23.2$ ($-25.5 < M_{1450} < -23.6$), extending quasar studies to the faint end of the quasar luminosity function (QLF) at $z \gtrsim 7$. The quasar with the highest-$z$, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1 at $z \approx 7.77$, sets the new redshift record for the most distant quasar ever reported. These discoveries demonstrate Euclid's transformative role in high-$z$ quasar discovery and set the stage for future follow-up studies of the early galaxies hosting quasars, supermassive black hole growth, and the intergalactic medium in the epoch of reionisation.

AI.motivation: To discover high-redshift quasars at z>6.6 using Euclid survey data to study early supermassive black hole growth, the quasar luminosity function at its faint end, and the intergalactic medium during the epoch of reionisation.
AI.method: Candidate selection via machine-learning and probabilistic techniques applied to Euclid I_E, Y_E, J_E, H_E images plus ancillary z-band data, followed by spectroscopic follow-up with Keck, Magellan, and LBT.
AI.result: 31 new quasars at 6.6<z<7.8; 12 at z≥7 (more than doubling known sample); magnitudes 21.2<J_E<23.2 (M_1450 from -25.5 to -23.6); highest-z quasar at z≈7.77.
AI.conclusion: Euclid demonstrates transformative capability for high-z quasar discovery, extending the QLF to fainter luminosities at z≳7 and enabling future studies of early galaxy-black hole co-evolution and reionisation-era IGM.

title: A NICER view of the millisecond pulsar PSR J2124$-$3358: evidence for a helium atmosphere
comment: 21 pages, 9 figures and 3 tables. Submitted to ApJ. Supplementary data products are available in Zenodo
summary: Pulse profile modeling has proven to be a powerful technique for determining the mass and radius of neutron stars. To date, this method has been applied to a handful of millisecond pulsars observed by the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER). However, analyses of more millisecond pulsars are necessary to determine tight constraints on the equation of state of superdense matter. In this study, we present an analysis of the isolated, rotation-powered millisecond pulsar PSR J2124$-$3358 using the X-ray Pulse Simulation and Inference (X-PSI) package, a publicly available state-of-the-art code for neutron-star relativistic ray tracing and Bayesian parameter inference. We use NICER and Chandra observations of this pulsar, exploring different neutron star atmospheric compositions and different configurations of the hot polar caps responsible for the pulsed X-ray emission. Our analyses favor a helium atmospheric composition, plausibly originating from accretion and subsequent evaporation of a former hydrogen-depleted binary companion. For this composition, and given the faint nature of the source and the low signal-to-noise of the data sets, we obtain broad posterior distributions yielding a mass $M = 1.8\pm0.5\,M_\odot$ and an equatorial radius $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = 11.7^{+2.6}_{-3.0}$ km (medians and $68\%$ credible intervals), and infer a configuration consisting of two slightly non-antipodal hot spots. By contrast, when using a hydrogen atmosphere model, the mass and radius decrease by $\sim 0.5\,M_\odot$ and $\sim 1$ km, respectively. Future multiwavelength studies, particularly those incorporating radio and gamma-ray pulse-emission, may provide tighter constraints on the geometry and physical properties of this source.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an analysis of the isolated millisecond pulsar PSR J2124-3358 using NICER and Chandra data with the X-PSI package. The analysis favors a helium atmosphere model, yielding broad posterior distributions with mass M=1.8±0.5 M☉ and equatorial radius Req=11.7+2.6-3.0 km, and two slightly non-antipodal hot spots. Hydrogen atmosphere models produce systematically lower mass and radius values.
AI.motivation: Determining tight constraints on the equation of state of superdense matter requires pulse profile modeling of more millisecond pulsars beyond those already analyzed by NICER.
AI.method: Applied the X-PSI (X-ray Pulse Simulation and Inference) package—a publicly available code for relativistic ray tracing and Bayesian parameter inference—to NICER and Chandra observations of PSR J2124-3358, exploring different atmospheric compositions (He vs. H) and hot polar cap configurations.
AI.result: Helium atmosphere favored; M=1.8±0.5 M☉, Req=11.7+2.6-3.0 km (medians and 68% credible intervals), with two slightly non-antipodal hot spots. Hydrogen atmosphere yields mass and radius lower by ~0.5 M☉ and ~1 km respectively.
AI.conclusion: Due to the faint nature and low signal-to-noise, posterior distributions are broad. Future multiwavelength studies (radio and gamma-ray) may provide tighter constraints on geometry and physical properties.

title: Discovery of a low surface brightness galaxy in the Zone of Avoidance using VVVX Deepstack imaging
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics Letters. This version includes the final minor revisions requested during the peer-review process
summary: We report the discovery of VVVX J080705.96-273823.6, the first low-surface-brightness galaxy candidate identified in the Zone of Avoidance by the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea eXtended Survey (VVVX). The source was detected serendipitously during a visual inspection of the new Deepstack images, reconstructed mosaics generated through an updated reprocessing and stacking procedure that significantly improves the depth and spatial uniformity of the original survey images. First-order morpho-photometric parameters were obtained using SExtractor together with PSF models derived with PSFEx, applied to star-subtracted images to minimize foreground contamination. Structural properties were derived from PSF-convolved modeling of azimuthally averaged surface-brightness profiles in the J, H, and Ks bands using exponential, Sersic, and composite models. The galaxy candidate is clearly detected in all three near-infrared bands. The profiles are consistently described by an exponential disk, with scale lengths of 32-36 arcsec and extinction-corrected central surface brightnesses of 19.82-22.35 mag arcsec^-2. The J band provides the best-constrained profile, while H and Ks show the same behavior with larger uncertainties. The projected proximity to ESO 494-25 and ESO 494-26 suggests a possible physical association. If located at the same distance (11-12 Mpc), the exponential scale length would be about 1.8-2.0 kpc, consistent with nearby LSB disk galaxies, although the lack of a spectroscopic redshift prevents confirmation. This discovery demonstrates that the new VVVX Deepstack products can reveal faint diffuse galaxies at low Galactic latitudes, opening a path toward a more complete census of the obscured nearby Universe.

It may be physically associated with ESO 494-25 and ESO 494-26 at ~11-12 Mpc, implying a ~1.8-2.0 kpc scale length, consistent with known LSB galaxies. No spectroscopic redshift is available yet.

AI.method: Serendipitous visual inspection of improved VVVX Deepstack mosaics (with enhanced depth and spatial uniformity). title: Neutron stars with an agnostic Dark sector: Core and Halo configurations from a two-fluid approach
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures
summary: The study of dark matter admixed neutron stars has the potential to advance our understanding of dark matter particle candidates. However, the large parameter space of dark matter particle masses restricts a systematic, model-independent study. In this analysis, we employ agnostic hadronic and dark matter equations of state to construct dark-matter-admixed neutron stars within a two-fluid formalism. Dark matter is characterised solely by its low-density equation of state and mass, and is modelled as a Fermi gas, while hadronic matter is anchored at low and high densities by chiral effective field theory and perturbative quantum chromodynamics calculations. A speed-of-sound parametrisation covers the intermediate density region for hadronic matter and the high-density region for dark matter, so the dark matter equation of state is constrained only by thermodynamic consistency, free from bias toward a softer or stiffer equation of state. Within this agnostic framework, we find that dark matter does not generically compactify the star: light dark matter forms extended halos that raise the tidal deformability, while heavy dark matter forms compact cores that lower it. Consequently, the dominant observational constraint shifts from gravitational-wave tidal deformability for light, halo-dominated models to NICER mass--radius data for heavy, core-dominated models. Using current data at $1σ$, we constrain the dark matter fraction to $f_{\mathrm{DM}} \lesssim 0.11$ for light dark matter. Being almost independent of any assumed dark-sector microphysics, our framework yields conservative, broadly applicable bounds on the dark-matter content of neutron stars. Neutron stars with similar masses but very different tidal deformabilities could be a smoking-gun signature of dark matter in Neutron stars.

Light dark matter forms extended halos increasing tidal deformability, while heavy dark matter forms compact cores decreasing it. Using current data at 1σ, the dark matter fraction is constrained to fDM ≲ 0.11 for light dark matter. Neutron stars with similar masses but different tidal deformabilities are proposed as a smoking-gun signature of dark matter.
AI.motivation: To advance understanding of dark matter particle candidates by studying dark matter admixed neutron stars, overcoming the challenge of the large parameter space of dark matter particle masses that restricts systematic, model-independent studies.
AI.method: Employ agnostic hadronic and dark matter equations of state within a two-fluid formalism. Dark matter is modeled as a Fermi gas characterized solely by its low-density equation of state and mass. Hadronic matter is anchored at low and high densities by chiral effective field theory and perturbative QCD, with a speed-of-sound parametrization covering intermediate densities for hadronic matter and high densities for dark matter. The dark matter equation of state is constrained only by thermodynamic consistency.
