The dominant observational constraint shifts from gravitational-wave tidal deformability (light, halo-dominated models) to NICER mass-radius data (heavy, core-dominated models). At 1σ, dark matter fraction is constrained to fDM ≲ 0.11 for light dark matter.
AI.conclusion: The agnostic framework yields conservative, broadly applicable bounds on the dark-matter content of neutron stars that are almost independent of any assumed dark-sector microphysics. Neutron stars with similar masses but very different tidal deformabilities could be a smoking-gun signature of dark matter in neutron stars.

title: Pebbles to Gems: Intermediate-mass black holes in the first star clusters
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Comments are welcome
summary: The rapid assembly of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) observed at $z\gtrsim7$ requires efficient seeding mechanisms in the early Universe. Population III (Pop. III) star clusters have recently emerged as a promising pathway that may bridge the gap between traditional light- and heavy-seed scenarios by producing intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) with masses up to $\sim10^4\,\rm M_{\odot}$. We investigate the properties and number densities of IMBHs forming in Pop. III star clusters with masses $M_{\rm cl}\sim10^3-4\times10^5\,\rm M_{\odot}$, and hosted in isolated dark matter minihalos, using a suite of direct $N$-body simulations. We adopt cosmologically motivated initial conditions and explore different stellar evolution prescriptions, binary orbital parameter distributions, and cluster dynamical configurations. By $z\sim19$, the IMBH mass function consistently peaks at $m_{\rm IMBH}\sim200\,\rm M_{\odot}$, with number densities of $n_{\rm IMBH}\sim0.2-5\,\rm cMpc^{-3}$. In sufficiently dense and massive clusters, IMBHs with masses $>10^3\,\rm M_{\odot}$ can already form by $z\sim19$, reaching number densities of $n_{\rm IMBH}\sim10^{-4}-10^{-2}\,\rm cMpc^{-3}$. The most massive IMBHs in our models reach $\sim6200\,\rm M_{\odot}$ through the collapse of very massive stars assembled by repeated stellar collisions, a process enhanced in fractal clusters. Lower-mass IMBHs form instead predominantly through single and binary stellar evolution and binary stellar mergers. We find that models combining large stellar radii and tight binaries produce the highest IMBH abundances relative to isolated Pop. III evolution. Owing to the high retention fraction of IMBHs ($\gtrsim88\%$), massive dense Pop. III star clusters can act as efficient incubators of both light and heavy SMBH seeds, even if only a fraction of Pop. III stars formed in such environments.

AI.tldr: Using N-body simulations, the authors show that Population III star clusters in minihalos can produce intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) up to ~6200 M☉ by z~19, with number densities of 0.2-5 cMpc⁻³ for ~200 M☉ IMBHs and 10⁻⁴-10⁻² cMpc⁻³ for >10³ M☉ IMBHs, serving as efficient seeds for supermassive black holes.
AI.motivation: The rapid assembly of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) at z≳7 requires efficient seeding mechanisms in the early Universe. The authors aim to bridge the gap between traditional light-seed (Pop. III remnants) and heavy-seed (direct collapse) scenarios by investigating Pop. III star clusters as a promising pathway to produce intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs).
AI.method: A suite of direct N-body simulations of Pop. III star clusters with masses M_cl ~ 10³–4×10⁵ M☉ hosted in isolated dark matter minihalos, using cosmologically motivated initial conditions and exploring different stellar evolution prescriptions, binary orbital parameter distributions, and cluster dynamical configurations.
AI.result: By z~19, the IMBH mass function peaks at ~200 M☉ with number densities 0.2-5 cMpc⁻³; IMBHs >10³ M☉ reach 10⁻⁴-10⁻² cMpc⁻³; the most massive IMBHs reach ~6200 M☉ via stellar collisions in fractal clusters; IMBH retention fraction is ≳88%.
AI.conclusion: Massive dense Pop. III star clusters can act as efficient incubators of both light and heavy SMBH seeds, even if only a fraction of Pop. III stars form in such environments, because of the high retention fraction and diverse formation channels (collisions, binary evolution, single stellar evolution).

title: Long-period radio transient PSR J0901-4046 is not an Isolated White Dwarf Pulsar
summary: We report the {\it Chandra} non-detection of PSR J0901$-$4046, a $P=75.89 $ seconds long-period radio transient (LPT). For a distance of 467 pc, the upper limit on X-ray luminosity is $L_X \leq$ few $\times 10^{28}$ erg s$^{-1}$. For the measured $P$ and $\dot{P}$, this upper limit, approximately 50 times lower than the previous {\it Swift} observations, is comparable to the spin-down luminosity of a neutron star, but would be approximately four orders of magnitude smaller than the spindown power of a white dwarf. Our results disfavor isolated WDs as the central star in PSR J0901$-$4046. We suggest that the isolated LPTs are powered by magnetic dissipation (not rotation), in a way similar to magnetars' radio emission.

AI.tldr: Chandra non-detection of LPT PSR J0901-4046 sets stringent X-ray upper limits (LX ≤ few ×10^28 erg/s), favoring a neutron star over a white dwarf, and suggesting magnetic dissipation (not rotation) as the power source for long-period radio transients.
AI.motivation: To determine the nature of the central object powering the long-period radio transient PSR J0901-4046 by obtaining sensitive X-ray constraints.
AI.method: Chandra X-ray observations of PSR J0901-4046 to measure or constrain its X-ray luminosity; comparison with spin-down luminosities of neutron stars and white dwarfs.
AI.result: X-ray upper limit ~50× lower than previous Swift observations; LX comparable to neutron star spin-down power but ~10^4× smaller than white dwarf spin-down power.
AI.conclusion: Isolated white dwarfs are disfavored as the central engine; isolated LPTs are likely powered by magnetic dissipation akin to magnetar radio emission rather than rotational energy.

title: A MIGHTEE robust measurement of the star formation rate-radio correlation
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Determining the relationship between star-formation rate (SFR) and the radio luminosity ($L_{1.4}$) is critical if we are to trace the star-formation history of the Universe dust-agnostically using current and future radio facilities. However, until now, such work has relied on potentially biased binary classifications of sources to remove contaminating active galactic nuclei (AGN). We present a new, statistically-driven methodology for deriving the SFR -- $L_{1.4}$ relation, removing the need for problematic cuts. We use a Bayesian hierarchical mixture model fit to the radio-detected sources in the deep MIGHTEE COSMOS DR1 catalogue, incorporating the full SFR posterior probability distributions generated by state-of-the-art spectral energy distribution fitting code \texttt{GRAHSP}. This allows us to probabilistically determine a mean SFR -- $L_{1.4}$ relation for the SF dominated galaxies, whilst accounting for changing fractions of SF dominated sources across redshift, radio luminosity and stellar mass ranges. We find that the SFR -- radio luminosity correlation exhibits a significant dependence on redshift, but a stellar mass dependence that is weaker than previous studies. Our resultant SFR-radio correlation is $\log_{10}(\text{SFR}/M_{\odot}\,\text{yr}^{-1}) = 0.790\times(\log _{10}(L_{1.4}/\text{W\,Hz}^{-1})-23) + 1.244 \times(1+z)^{0.122} -0.033 \times (\log_{10}(M_*/M_{\odot})-10)$, with an intrinsic scatter of 0.178 dex. We show that this redshift evolution could be explained by a moderate evolution in the radio spectral index of SF galaxies. We attribute the lack of observed strong dependence on stellar mass, compared to recent studies, to the novel statistical approach that does not rely on cuts to remove AGN.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a statistically-driven Bayesian hierarchical mixture model to derive the SFR–radio luminosity relation without needing binary AGN classification cuts. Using MIGHTEE COSMOS DR1 data, they find a significant redshift dependence but weaker stellar mass dependence in the relation, with the redshift evolution possibly due to moderate changes in radio spectral index.
AI.motivation: Determining the SFR–$L_{1.4}$ relation is critical for dust-agnostic star-formation history studies using radio facilities, but prior work relied on potentially biased binary AGN removal classifications.
AI.method: Bayesian hierarchical mixture model applied to MIGHTEE COSMOS DR1 radio-detected sources, incorporating full SFR posterior distributions from GRAHSP to probabilistically derive the mean SFR–$L_{1.4}$ relation for star-formation-dominated galaxies while accounting for varying fractions across redshift, radio luminosity, and stellar mass.
AI.result: SFR–radio correlation: $\log_{10}(\text{SFR}) = 0.790(\log_{10}(L_{1.4})-23) + 1.244(1+z)^{0.122} -0.033(\log_{10}(M_*/M_{\odot})-10)$, intrinsic scatter 0.178 dex. Significant redshift dependence; weaker stellar mass dependence than previous studies.
AI.conclusion: The redshift evolution may be explained by moderate evolution in the radio spectral index of SF galaxies. The lack of strong stellar mass dependence is attributed to the novel statistical approach avoiding AGN removal cuts.

title: Cross-validation of six dispersion measure estimation methods for FRB 20240114A
comment: 13 pages, 16 figures
summary: Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are important cosmological probes, but their applications depend critically on accurate dispersion measure (DM) determinations. We present a systematic comparison of six DM estimation methods using 2,874 bursts from FRB20240114A, the most active repeating FRB currently known, observed by FAST during a single 4.4-hr session on 2024 March 12. This large, homogeneous sample over a short timescale, during which the propagation environment is expected to be nearly static, provides an ideal benchmark for isolating algorithmic effects on DM determination. We investigate the dependence of inter-method consistency on signal-to-noise ratio (S/N), burst morphology, and radio frequency interference (RFI). Low-S/N bursts exhibit significantly larger inter-method deviations, while single-component bursts produce highly consistent DM values across methods. In contrast, complex double- and multiple-component bursts with drifting substructures lead to substantial inter-method scattering, indicating that DM discrepancies are primarily driven by algorithmic responses to burst morphology. RFI does not significantly alter the global statistical behavior of DM deviations, but it affects density-filtering methods through morphology distortion caused by frequency-channel masking. Even after imposing strict inter-method consistency constraints, FRB20240114A still exhibits notable apparent DM fluctuations spanning $\sim$528-534~pc~cm$^{-3}$ over 15,780s. For morphologically simple bursts these variations far exceed the measurement uncertainty and, on second-to-minute timescales, cannot arise from any plausible change in the line-of-sight electron column, pointing instead to a frequency-dependent emission-time structure intrinsic to the bursts that mimics dispersion.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares six dispersion measure (DM) estimation methods using 2,874 bursts from the highly active repeating FRB20240114A observed by FAST during a single 4.4-hour session. It finds that inter-method DM consistency depends strongly on burst S/N and morphology: low-S/N bursts and multi-component bursts produce larger DM discrepancies, while RFI has minimal global effect. Even after stringent consistency filtering, the source shows apparent DM fluctuations (~528-534 pc cm⁻³) that exceed measurement uncertainty on short timescales, which cannot be explained by line-of-sight electron column changes, suggesting intrinsic frequency-dependent emission-time structure mimics dispersion.
AI.motivation: FRBs are important cosmological probes whose applications critically depend on accurate dispersion measure (DM) determinations. However, the reliability of different DM estimation methods and the sources of inter-method discrepancies have not been systematically evaluated on a large, homogeneous dataset.
AI.method: The authors used 2,874 bursts from FRB20240114A observed by FAST during a single 4.4-hour session (March 12, 2024). They systematically compared six DM estimation methods, analyzing how inter-method consistency depends on signal-to-noise ratio (S/N), burst morphology (single-, double-, and multiple-component), and radio frequency interference (RFI).
AI.result: Low-S/N bursts show larger inter-method DM deviations. Single-component bursts yield highly consistent DMs across methods, while complex multi-component bursts with drifting substructures cause substantial inter-method scattering. RFI does not significantly alter global DM statistics but affects density-filtering methods via morphology distortion. After imposing strict consistency constraints, FRB20240114A still exhibits apparent DM fluctuations (528-534 pc cm⁻³) over 15,780 seconds that far exceed measurement uncertainty on short timescales.
AI.conclusion: DM discrepancies are primarily driven by algorithmic responses to burst morphology, not RFI. The observed apparent DM fluctuations on second-to-minute timescales cannot arise from plausible changes in line-of-sight electron column density, suggesting they originate from intrinsic frequency-dependent emission-time structure in the bursts that mimics dispersion.

title: From Atomic Gas to Star Formation
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Rosolowsky01
summary: Since the 2015 SKA Chapters, the advent of panchromatic observations of nearby galaxies, capable of resolving the interstellar medium (ISM) into individual star-forming regions and molecular clouds, has revolutionized our understanding of the star formation cycle in galaxies. Despite these advances, our understanding of the gas cycle in galaxies remains limited because we know little about how the cold atomic phase of the ISM, which dominates its mass budget, participates in the cycle. Specifically, the processes regulating the condensation of atomic gas into molecular gas, the balance between warm and cold atomic gas, and their dependence on local environment and star formation activity have been explored only in the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds. The SKA presents a new opportunity to observe the atomic ISM within nearby galaxies at comparable resolution to other facilities and is the only facility that can make wide-area surveys of atomic gas across a statistical sample of galaxies at high (<100 pc) spatial resolution. Such observations will directly address the open questions about the evolution of the star-forming ISM. We present recent results from SKA-like observations of the Local Group made with SKA pathfinders and the Jansky VLA to illustrate the promise of replicating those observations for hundreds of nearby galaxies, reaching out to the Virgo cluster.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses how high-resolution panchromatic observations have revolutionized our understanding of the star formation cycle, but the cold atomic gas phase remains poorly understood. SKA offers the unique capability to map atomic ISM at <100 pc resolution across a large sample of nearby galaxies, addressing key questions about gas condensation and phase balance. Results from SKA pathfinders and VLA observations of the Local Group demonstrate the potential for expanding such studies to hundreds of galaxies out to the Virgo cluster.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of cold atomic gas in the star formation cycle, specifically how atomic gas condenses into molecular gas, how warm and cold atomic gas phases are balanced, and how these processes depend on local environment and star formation activity beyond the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds.
AI.method: Using SKA-like observations from SKA pathfinders and the Jansky VLA to observe the atomic ISM in nearby galaxies at high (<100 pc) spatial resolution, comparable to other panchromatic facilities.
AI.result: SKA pathfinder and VLA observations of the Local Group demonstrate the feasibility of replicating high-resolution atomic gas studies for hundreds of nearby galaxies out to the Virgo cluster.
AI.conclusion: The SKA is uniquely capable of conducting wide-area, high-resolution surveys of atomic gas across a statistically significant sample of galaxies, which will directly address open questions about the evolution of the star-forming ISM and the atomic-to-molecular gas transition.

title: Constraining Pulsar Radiative Geometry via Multi-wavelength Modeling
summary: We propose that jointly modeling the thermal X-ray pulse profiles and the polarization position angles offers an effective means of locating the polarization orientation focus of the pulsar's coherent radiation. From the X-ray pulse-profile measurement we constrain the colatitude of the center of the thermal X-ray emission, which corresponds to the center of in-falling particles within the polar cap, while the RVM fitting yields the inclination angle of the focus point of polarization orientations. Thus, consistency between these two independent angle measurements would imply that the RVM fit faithfully recovers the inclination of the plasma flow center, and this center coincides with the polarization orientation focus. Conversely, the discrepancy would suggest that the polarization state of the radio emission changes as it propagates because the evolution of wave modes during wave propagation in the magnetosphere strongly depends on magnetic field orientations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes combining thermal X-ray pulse-profiles and polarization position angles to locate the polarization orientation focus of pulsar coherent radiation, and using consistency between these measurements to test whether radio emission polarization is affected by propagation effects in the magnetosphere.
AI.motivation: To develop a method for locating the polarization orientation focus of a pulsar's coherent radiation and to understand whether the polarization state of radio emission is modified by propagation effects in the magnetosphere.
AI.method: Joint modeling of thermal X-ray pulse profiles (to constrain the colatitude of thermal X-ray emission center, i.e., the polar cap particle infall center) and polarization position angles via RVM fitting (to obtain the inclination angle of the polarization orientation focus). Consistency between these two independent angle measurements is used as a diagnostic.
AI.result: If the two angle measurements are consistent, the RVM fit faithfully recovers the inclination of the plasma flow center, which coincides with the polarization orientation focus. If they are discrepant, the polarization state of radio emission changes during propagation due to wave mode evolution depending on magnetic field orientations.
AI.conclusion: Joint modeling of X-ray pulse profiles and polarization position angles is an effective way to locate the polarization orientation focus and test for propagation-induced polarization changes in pulsar magnetospheres.

title: A population of LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA mergers happening inside active galactic nuclei
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures
summary: Multimessenger observations of compact binary mergers in active galactic nuclei (AGN) offer unique probes of black hole formation channels and cosmology. We analyse 18 gravitational-wave events from LVK observing runs O3--O4b paired with 28 candidate AGN counterparts, incorporating supermassive black hole (SMBH)-induced environmental redshift corrections and electromagnetic sky-localisation constraints. Of the 28 candidate pairs, 21 are positive-to-strong-favoured (the most compelling being GW190412\_053044 $\leftrightarrow$ J143041.67$+$355703.8 at $\ln\mathcal{B} = +17.35$), three are inconclusive, and four are negative-to-strong-disfavoured. From the 21 positive-to-strong-favoured binary black hole (BBH) AGN pairs, 13 unique associations can be identified as the preferred ones. The cumulative Bayes factor across all 13 BBH-AGN confirmed associations yields $\ln\mathcal{B}_{\rm comb} \approx +81$, establishing strong collective support for AGN-hosted merger associations. Sky localisation is the dominant driver of model selection; at current detector sensitivity, the environmental redshift corrections are neither decisively confirmed nor ruled out, motivating future high-precision multimessenger follow-up.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 18 gravitational-wave events from LVK O3–O4b paired with 28 AGN candidates, finding strong collective support (lnB_comb ≈ +81) for 13 unique BBH-AGN associations, with sky localisation being the key factor rather than environmental redshift corrections.
AI.motivation: To use multimessenger observations of compact binary mergers in AGN to probe black hole formation channels and cosmology, by evaluating AGN associations as potential host environments for gravitational-wave events.
AI.method: Analyzed 18 GW events from LVK O3–O4b with 28 candidate AGN counterparts, incorporating SMBH-induced environmental redshift corrections and electromagnetic sky-localisation constraints; used Bayes factors to assess association strength.
AI.result: 21 of 28 candidate pairs are positive-to-strong-favoured (most compelling: GW190412_053044 ↔ J143041.67+355703.8, lnB=+17.35), 3 inconclusive, 4 negative-to-strong-disfavoured; 13 unique associations identified; cumulative lnB_comb ≈ +81 across all confirmed associations.
AI.conclusion: There is strong collective support for AGN-hosted merger associations. Sky localisation is the dominant model selection driver; environmental redshift corrections remain inconclusive at current sensitivity, motivating future high-precision multimessenger follow-up.

title: Measuring the Angular Auto-power Spectrum of Fast Radio Burst Dispersion Measures as a Robust Cosmological Probe and Baryon Tracer
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures
summary: Fluctuations in the cosmic electron density are imprinted on the dispersion measures (DMs) of fast radio bursts (FRBs), making DMs a promising probe of cosmology and the spatial distribution of ionized baryons. In this work, we present the first measurement of the angular auto-power spectrum of FRB DMs, using 3455 apparently non-repeating bursts from the CHIME/FRB Catalog 2. We detect an angular correlation signal at $>3σ$ significance, associated with large-scale electron-density fluctuations. By fitting the measured spectrum to theoretical models, we constrain two key parameter combinations: $Ω_{\rm b}h^2$-$H_0$, which probes the cosmic baryon density and expansion rate, and $Ω_{\rm b}h^2$-$f_{\rm d}$, which traces the baryon fraction in cosmic large-scale structure (LSS). We further assess the robustness of the power-spectrum method against systematic uncertainties arising from the assumed FRB redshift distribution and from the DM contributions of host galaxies (${\rm DM}_{\rm host}$), the Galactic halo (${\rm DM}^{\rm MW}_{\rm halo}$), and the Milky Way interstellar medium (${\rm DM}^{\rm MW}_{\rm ISM}$), using mock samples. Our results demonstrate that the angular power spectrum is largely insensitive to uncorrelated DM components such as ${\rm DM}_{\rm host}$, thereby effectively mitigating the impact of poorly constrained host-galaxy systematics. In contrast to the traditional ${\rm DM}_{\rm LSS}$-$z$ relation, this method does not require individual redshift measurements--it relies only on the overall redshift distribution--and it partially breaks the parameter degeneracies in the $Ω_{\rm b}h^2$-$H_0$ and $Ω_{\rm b}h^2$-$f_{\rm d}$ planes. These findings establish the DM angular power spectrum as a robust cosmological probe and a powerful baryon tracer.

AI.tldr: Using 3,455 FRBs from CHIME/FRB Catalog 2, this work presents the first measurement of the angular auto-power spectrum of FRB dispersion measures, detecting a >3σ angular correlation signal. The method constrains Ω_b h²-H₀ and Ω_b h²-f_d, is robust to host-galaxy systematics, and does not require individual redshift measurements.
AI.motivation: FRB DMs encode fluctuations in cosmic electron density, offering a probe of cosmology and the distribution of ionized baryons in large-scale structure. Traditional approaches require individual redshift measurements and suffer from host-galaxy systematic uncertainties.
AI.method: The angular auto-power spectrum of FRB DMs is measured from 3,455 non-repeating CHIME/FRB bursts. Theoretical models are fitted to constrain Ω_b h²-H₀ and Ω_b h²-f_d. Robustness is assessed via mock samples against systematics from FRB redshift distribution, DM_host, DM_halo^MW, and DM_ISM^MW.
AI.result: Detection of angular correlation at >3σ significance. The power spectrum is largely insensitive to uncorrelated DM components (e.g., DM_host), mitigating host-galaxy systematics. The method partially breaks degeneracies in the Ω_b h²-H₀ and Ω_b h²-f_d parameter planes.
AI.conclusion: The FRB DM angular power spectrum is established as a robust cosmological probe and a powerful baryon tracer, requiring only the overall redshift distribution rather than per-burst redshifts.

title: Exploring the Influence of the Jet-environment Interactions on the Observed Asymmetry of Extragalactic Radio Sources with SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/SabyasachiPal03
summary: Several observational and theoretical studies have suggested that the observed arm-length asymmetries in extragalactic radio sources are primarily driven by interactions between radio jets and an inhomogeneous ambient medium, although orientation effects may also contribute to the observed asymmetry. However, the observational evidence supporting these interpretations comes from only a small sample of FR II radio sources, in which the brighter hotspots are typically found on the side of the shorter jet arm. We aim to investigate the interactions between powerful jets and their surrounding environments in radio sources, with a particular focus on how these interactions shape the morphology and asymmetry of the radio lobes. The unprecedented sensitivity and angular resolution of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) will facilitate the discovery and detailed characterization of asymmetric radio sources across a wide range of physical scales and redshifts. Using a combination of 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations and observational data from the SKAO, one can explore the influence of clumpy interstellar and intergalactic media on jet propagation and the resulting asymmetries in radio sources at various redshifts. The study will analyze how environmental factors, such as density and turbulence, decelerate jets, leading to observable asymmetries in smaller, higher-redshift sources. In this chapter, we review existing simulation and observational results on jet-environment interactions in radio galaxies and discuss how SKAO capabilities will further advance our understanding of AGN feedback and its role in shaping large-scale cosmic structure.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews how arm-length asymmetries in extragalactic radio sources are driven by jet-environment interactions, and discusses how future SKAO observations combined with 3D MHD simulations will improve our understanding of AGN feedback and its role in shaping large-scale cosmic structure.
AI.motivation: Observational evidence of arm-length asymmetries is limited to a small sample of FR II radio sources, and the underlying physical mechanisms (jet-environment interactions vs. orientation effects) remain poorly constrained. The authors aim to address this gap by leveraging SKAO's sensitivity and resolution to systematically study asymmetric radio sources across a wide range of redshifts.
AI.method: The study proposes combining 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations with observational data from the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) to model jet propagation through clumpy interstellar and intergalactic media, and to analyze how environmental factors (density, turbulence) decelerate jets and produce asymmetries.
AI.result: The paper does not present new results; it reviews existing simulation and observational findings on jet-environment interactions and outlines the anticipated capabilities of SKAO for future studies.
AI.conclusion: SKAO's unprecedented sensitivity and angular resolution will enable detailed characterization of asymmetric radio sources, advancing our understanding of AGN feedback and its impact on large-scale cosmic structure formation.

title: Exploring Hierarchical Merger Scenarios for GW241011 and GW241110
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures
summary: GW241011 and GW241110 are asymmetric binary black hole mergers with rapidly spinning primaries, unequal component masses, and nonzero spin--orbit tilts, making them natural candidates for hierarchical mergers. We use a Bayesian framework to compare a fiducial first-generation (1G+1G) binary black hole population with second-generation plus first-generation (2G+1G) hierarchical merger models in star clusters and active galactic nucleus (AGN) disks. Both events favor the 2G+1G interpretation over the 1G+1G hypothesis, with $\ln\mathcal{B}^{\rm 2G+1G}_{\rm 1G+1G}\simeq6.5$--$8.6$ for GW241011 and $\ln\mathcal{B}^{\rm 2G+1G}_{\rm 1G+1G}\simeq3.0$--$4.5$ for GW241110, depending on the waveform model and assumed environment. The AGN disk models yields slightly larger evidence than the star cluster models, mainly due to their spin tilt distribution, but the data do not provide a decisive environmental classification. We further consider a third-generation plus first-generation (3G+1G) interpretation, but it is not robustly preferred over 2G+1G scenarios. Finally, we also search for optical counterparts by examining AGNs within the three-dimensional localization volumes using ZTF and ATLAS forced photometry, and find one candidate source with weak flare, which might be associated with GW241110 event.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes GW241011 and GW241110 as asymmetric binary black hole mergers, finding they favor second-generation+first-generation hierarchical merger interpretations over standard first-generation models, with Bayesian evidences showing log Bayes factors of 6.5-8.6 and 3.0-4.5 respectively. The study also searches for optical counterparts and identifies one candidate AGN flare possibly associated with GW241110.
AI.motivation: To determine whether GW241011 and GW241110—asymmetric binary black hole mergers with rapidly spinning primaries, unequal masses, and nonzero spin-orbit tilts—originate from hierarchical mergers (2G+1G) rather than standard first-generation formation channels, and to identify potential electromagnetic counterparts.
AI.method: Bayesian framework comparing fiducial 1G+1G population models with 2G+1G hierarchical merger models in star clusters and AGN disks; additionally, 3G+1G models were tested, and optical counterpart searches were conducted via ZTF and ATLAS forced photometry of AGNs within localization volumes.
AI.result: Both events favor 2G+1G over 1G+1G (ln Bayes factor ~6.5-8.6 for GW241011, ~3.0-4.5 for GW241110). AGN disk models yield slightly higher evidence than star cluster models. 3G+1G is not robustly preferred over 2G+1G. One candidate AGN flare possibly associated with GW241110 was identified.
AI.conclusion: GW241011 and GW241110 are likely hierarchical mergers (2G+1G) rather than first-generation binaries. The AGN channel is slightly favored over star clusters but not decisively. No strong evidence for a 3G+1G scenario, and one potential electromagnetic counterpart for GW241110 warrants further investigation.

title: Tracing the Origin of Circular-Symmetry Diffuse Radio Sources in the Next-Generation SKAO Era
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/SabyasachiPal02
summary: Circularly symmetric diffuse radio sources represent a recently recognized and rare class of extragalactic synchrotron-emitting structures whose physical origin remains uncertain. The currently known population is small, and the limited frequency coverage, sensitivity, and polarimetric information available from existing observations hinder robust discrimination among the various proposed formation scenarios. This chapter presents an overview of four representative circular diffuse sources featuring diverse morphologies, such as a horseshoe-shaped inner ring, circular diffuse emission surrounded by inner S/Z-shaped structures and a double-ring diffuse source. The angular sizes of these sources are in the range of 60-100 arcsec, similar to odd radio circles (ORCs). These systems illustrate the morphological diversity of circular diffuse radio emission and provide valuable clues to the physical processes responsible for their formation. The Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO), with its unprecedented sensitivity, wide instantaneous bandwidth, sub-arcsecond imaging capability, and high-fidelity polarimetric performance, will significantly advance the study of these objects. SKAO surveys are expected to detect a substantially larger population of faint circular diffuse radio sources, enabling the first statistically meaningful studies of their occurrence, environments, and evolution. An expanded sample will allow investigations of their cosmological evolution and help determine whether their origin is linked to AGN feedback processes, episodic jet activity, galaxy interactions, or large-scale structure formation. This chapter summarizes the current observational knowledge of circular diffuse radio sources and describes how next-generation radio facilities, particularly the SKAO, will enable progress in understanding the origin and physical nature of these enigmatic radio structures.

AI.tldr: Circularly symmetric diffuse radio sources are rare extragalactic synchrotron-emitting structures with unknown origins. This chapter reviews four representative sources (60-100 arcsec, similar to odd radio circles), highlighting their morphological diversity. SKAO's enhanced sensitivity, bandwidth, resolution, and polarimetry will enable detection of larger populations, statistical studies, and discrimination among formation scenarios (AGN feedback, jet activity, galaxy interactions, structure formation).
AI.motivation: Circularly symmetric diffuse radio sources are rare and poorly understood; their physical origin remains uncertain due to limited observational data (small sample, narrow frequency coverage, insufficient sensitivity and polarimetry).
AI.method: Overview of four representative circular diffuse sources with diverse morphologies (horseshoe-shaped inner ring, S/Z-shaped structures, double-ring), compared to odd radio circles (ORCs) in angular size (60-100 arcsec).
AI.result: These sources exhibit significant morphological diversity, providing clues to their formation. SKAO will enable detection of larger populations and statistically meaningful studies of their occurrence, environments, and evolution.
AI.conclusion: Next-generation radio facilities, particularly SKAO, will resolve the origin of these enigmatic structures by enabling investigations of cosmological evolution and discriminating between AGN feedback, episodic jet activity, galaxy interactions, and large-scale structure formation scenarios.

title: Evidence for a Delayed Progenitor Population for CHIME non-repeating Fast Radio Bursts using a Self-Consistent Forward and Backward Inference Framework
comment: Submitted; 13 pages, 8 figures; comments are welcome!
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are luminous extragalactic radio transients whose physical origins remain uncertain. Using over one thousand non-repeating events from CHIME/FRB Catalog 2, we infer the intrinsic FRB demographics with a self-consistent framework that combines backward non-parametric inference and forward population synthesis while accounting for probabilistic dispersion measure--redshift estimates, baseband-to-catalog fluence corrections, and the latest fuzzy multidimensional selection function. We first apply a backward non-parametric method, the weighted Lynden--Bell $C^{-}$ estimator, to recover the intrinsic redshift and energy distributions without assuming any population model. Independently, we perform forward Monte Carlo population synthesis in observable dispersion measure--fluence space, treating candidate intrinsic redshift and energy distributions as population hypotheses and comparing the resulting selected synthetic catalogs with observations. We find that the intrinsic redshift distribution peaks at $z\sim1$, significantly lower than the cosmic star formation history (SFH) peak at $z\sim1.7$, indicating clear tension with a pure SFH-tracking scenario, suggesting that at least some FRBs are delayed with respect to SFH. The intrinsic energy distribution is consistent with a power law of index $α\approx1.9$ and steepens at higher energies. We find no significant evidence for a redshift-energy distribution correlation.

AI.tldr: Using over 1000 non-repeating FRBs from CHIME/FRB Catalog 2, this study infers intrinsic FRB demographics via backward non-parametric inference and forward population synthesis. The intrinsic redshift distribution peaks at z~1, lower than the cosmic SFH peak (z~1.7), suggesting delayed FRB origins. The energy distribution follows a power law (α~1.9) steepening at high energies, with no significant redshift-energy correlation.
AI.motivation: To infer the intrinsic demographics (redshift and energy distributions) of non-repeating FRBs using a large catalog, and to test whether FRB rate tracks the cosmic star formation history or requires a delayed channel.
AI.method: Combined backward non-parametric inference (weighted Lynden-Bell C⁻ estimator) and forward Monte Carlo population synthesis in observable DM-fluence space, with probabilistic DM–redshift estimates, baseband-to-catalog fluence corrections, and a fuzzy multidimensional selection function.
AI.result: Intrinsic redshift distribution peaks at z~1 (below SFH peak at z~1.7, tension with pure SFH-tracking); energy distribution is a power law with index α≈1.9 steepening at high energies; no significant redshift-energy correlation.
AI.conclusion: FRBs are not simple tracers of cosmic star formation; at least some FRB progenitors involve a delayed channel relative to SFH.

title: A Homogeneous Determination of the Interstellar Extinction Law and Metallicity for 105 Galactic Open Clusters
summary: This work presents an investigation of the interstellar extinction law toward 105 Galactic open clusters using ultraviolet-optical photometry. The photometric dataset and reddening determinations were previously introduced in Ramezani et al., (2025); hereafter Paper I, where homogeneous ultraviolet photometry and colour-colour diagrams were used to derive reddening values for the cluster sample. In the present study, we extend that analysis by determining extinction law and metallicity parameters for the same clusters. Ground-based U-band observations obtained with the 2.15-m CASLEO telescope and the 1.54-m Danish telescope are combined with Gaia Data Release 3 photometry to construct ultraviolet-optical colour indices. Using extinction-ratio combinations and the Fitzpatrick, (1999) extinction model, we derive mean total-to-selective extinction law values (RV) for all clusters. The resulting RV values span approximately 2.5-4.5, with a mean value of RV = 3.53, indicating significant spatial variations of dust properties across the Galactic disk and deviations from the canonical diffuse interstellar medium value RV = 3.1. Afterward, by fitting the isochrone to the Colour-Magnitude Diagrams, we estimated the metallicity values of 105 observed clusters. This work provides the first homogeneous catalogue of extinction law measurements based on combined ground-based ultraviolet and Gaia photometry for a large open-cluster sample, establishing an important reference for studies of Galactic dust structure and stellar parameter corrections.

AI.tldr: This study determines interstellar extinction law (RV) and metallicity parameters for 105 Galactic open clusters using ground-based U-band (CASLEO/Danish telescopes) + Gaia DR3 photometry, finding RV values ranging ~2.5–4.5 (mean 3.53) and providing the first homogeneous UV+Gaia extinction catalogue for open clusters.
AI.motivation: To extend prior reddening work (Paper I) by deriving extinction law and metallicity parameters for a large sample of open clusters, addressing the lack of homogeneous UV-optical extinction measurements for Galactic dust structure studies.
AI.method: Combined ground-based U-band (CASLEO 2.15-m, Danish 1.54-m) with Gaia DR3 photometry to construct UV-optical colour indices; used extinction-ratio combinations and the Fitzpatrick (1999) extinction model to derive RV values; fitted isochrones to CMDs for metallicity estimation.
AI.result: RV values span ~2.5–4.5 with mean RV = 3.53, indicating significant spatial dust property variations across the Galactic disk and deviations from the canonical diffuse ISM value (RV = 3.1). Metallicity values estimated for all 105 clusters.
AI.conclusion: Provides the first homogeneous catalogue of extinction law measurements based on combined ground-based ultraviolet and Gaia photometry for a large open-cluster sample, establishing an important reference for studies of Galactic dust structure and stellar parameter corrections.

title: An 18-year Fermi-LAT stacking limit on GeV $γ$-ray emission from particle-accelerating colliding-wind binaries
comment: Prepared for submission to JCAP
summary: The wind-collision regions of massive colliding-wind binaries (CWBs) accelerate relativistic particles, as shown by their non-thermal radio synchrotron and, in $η$ Car, hard X-ray emission. Whether CWBs emit GeV $γ$rays as a population is unknown: only $η$ Car is unambiguously detected by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT). We analyze 17.8 yr of Fermi-LAT data above 1 GeV (where the sharp point-spread function controls plane confusion) at the 61 confirmed (list A) particle-accelerating CWBs (PACWBs) of De Becker & Raucq, using a two-dimensional (photon index $\times$ flux) likelihood scan against 200 control fields matched in latitude, local source density, and diffuse intensity. Removing systems whose lines of sight coincide with bright catalogue $γ$-ray sources leaves a clean, mutually isolated sample of 6, whose stack is consistent with the control-field null ($p=0.83$): no evidence for collective GeV emission. Retaining those systems instead yields a spurious $\gtrsim3.5σ$ excess from chance catalogue coincidences, a caveat for Galactic-plane stacking. The resulting 95% limit on the mean per-source flux, $F(>1\,\mathrm{GeV})\lesssim1.1\times10^{-11}~\mathrm{ph\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}} (Γ=2)$, implies a $γ$-ray production efficiency $η=L_γ/L_{\rm wind}\lesssim4\times10^{-6}\,(d/\mathrm{kpc})^2$, about two orders of magnitude below $η$ Car at the sample's median distance. A representative single-zone model then bounds the electron acceleration efficiency in CWB wind-collision regions unless their magnetic field is comparable to or above the magnetic-photon equipartition value. Among the high-latitude systems accessible to a clean stack, $η$ Car thus appears to be a singular object rather than the brightest member of an emerging population.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 17.8 yr of Fermi-LAT data for 61 particle-accelerating colliding-wind binaries finds no collective GeV γ-ray emission; only η Car is detected, with a derived efficiency limit ~100× below η Car, suggesting it is a singular object rather than the brightest of an emerging population.
AI.motivation: To determine whether massive colliding-wind binaries (CWBs) as a population emit GeV γ-rays, given that only η Car is unambiguously detected, and to constrain the acceleration efficiency of relativistic particles in these systems.
AI.method: Analyzed 17.8 yr of Fermi-LAT data (>1 GeV) for 61 confirmed particle-accelerating CWBs using a 2D (photon index × flux) likelihood scan against 200 control fields matched in latitude, source density, and diffuse intensity; performed clean stack of systems free of bright catalogue γ-ray sources, and a separate stacked analysis retaining all systems.
AI.result: Clean, mutually isolated sample of 6 systems shows no evidence of collective GeV emission (p=0.83). Retaining all systems yields spurious ~3.5σ excess from chance catalogue coincidences. 95% flux limit: F(>1 GeV) ≲ 1.1×10⁻¹¹ ph cm⁻² s⁻¹ (Γ=2), implying γ-ray efficiency η = L_γ/L_wind ≲ 4×10⁻⁶ (d/kpc)², ~100× below η Car at median distance.
AI.conclusion: η Car appears to be a singular object among CWBs in GeV γ-ray emission, not the brightest of an emerging population. The electron acceleration efficiency in CWB wind-collision regions is bounded unless magnetic fields are at or above equipartition.

title: Excitation of warm HD and H$_2$ and implications for the interstellar deuterium abundance
comment: 38 pages including 14 figures. Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: Rotational emission from HD provides a direct probe of deuterium in warm molecular gas, but the conversion of HD line fluxes to total column densities is sensitive to non-LTE excitation. I present calculations of the non-LTE rotational excitation of HD and H$_2$ and a method for fitting their rotational diagrams simultaneously. Because HD remains subthermally excited to higher densities than H$_2$, the combined analysis constrains the thermal pressure as well as the HD/H$_2$ abundance ratio. I apply this method to JWST/MIRI observations of 26 positions in 10 protostellar outflows from the JOYS survey, published previously by Francis et al. (2025), including 17 positions with secure detections of at least three HD lines. Two-temperature, isobaric models generally provide good fits to the measured H$_2$ and HD level populations. For 11 positions with HD detections, the inferred pressures span $p/k_B=8.4\times10^7$ - $5.1\times10^9\ {\rm K\,cm^{-3}}$; for the remaining six, the HD populations approach LTE and provide only lower limits on the gas pressure. Excluding two positions toward IRAS 4B with comparatively poor fits, the median and mean inferred HD/H$_2$ abundance ratios are $1.42\times10^{-5}$ and $1.47\times10^{-5}$, respectively, only 28$\%$ and 29$\%$ of the value expected if all primordial deuterium were present as HD. These results confirm that HD/H$_2$ is generally low in shocked molecular gas while demonstrating that pressure-dependent non-LTE excitation must be modeled explicitly. Translating the measured HD/H$_2$ ratios into elemental D/H requires additional modeling of shock chemistry.

AI.tldr: This paper presents non-LTE calculations for HD rotational excitation and a method to simultaneously fit HD and H₂ rotational diagrams, applied to JWST/MIRI observations of 26 positions in protostellar outflows. The analysis constrains thermal pressure and HD/H₂ abundance ratios, finding median HD/H₂ = 1.42×10⁻⁵ (28% of primordial value), confirming HD is generally depleted in shocked molecular gas.
AI.motivation: To use rotational emission from HD as a direct probe of deuterium in warm molecular gas, but non-LTE excitation complicates the conversion of line fluxes to column densities. A method is needed to simultaneously constrain HD/H₂ abundance ratios and thermal pressure.
AI.method: Non-LTE rotational excitation calculations for HD and H₂ are performed. A two-temperature, isobaric model fitting approach is applied to simultaneous rotational diagram analysis of both species, using JWST/MIRI observations from the JOYS survey (26 positions in 10 protostellar outflows).
AI.result: 17 positions with ≥3 HD line detections. Pressures span p/k_B = 8.4×10⁷–5.1×10⁹ K cm⁻³ (11 positions); 6 positions give only lower limits. Median HD/H₂ = 1.42×10⁻⁵, mean = 1.47×10⁻⁵ (28% and 29% of primordial expectation).
AI.conclusion: HD/H₂ is generally low in shocked molecular gas, confirming deuterium depletion; pressure-dependent non-LTE excitation must be explicitly modeled. Translating HD/H₂ to elemental D/H requires additional shock chemistry modeling.

title: Spectropolarimetric detection of baryonic mass loading in a transient relativistic jet: application to the black hole X-ray binary Swift J1727.8$-$1613
comment: 29 pages, 15 figures, and 1 table, with an additional 10-page appendix containing 7 figures and 2 tables. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Radio emission during X-ray binary outbursts is dominated by synchrotron radiation from relativistic jets, but is usually studied through total-intensity diagnostics such as flux density, spectra, variability, and proper motion. Radio spectropolarimetry provides a complementary probe of the magneto-ionic plasma through Faraday rotation and depolarisation. When the Faraday rotating material is local to the source, these effects can constrain the jet plasma composition and mass content, but this approach is rarely applied to transient jetted sources. We present MeerKAT L-band spectropolarimetry of the black hole X-ray binary \src\ during its 2023 outburst, focusing on the brightest radio flaring interval, when relativistic jets were being launched intermittently. Using multiple spectropolarimetric techniques, we identify transient Faraday-complex structure coincident with the major radio flares. The close temporal association with the flaring activity, together with the stability of the foreground Faraday screen, favours an origin local to the jet rather than in the ISM or in a separate local screen external to the emitting plasma. Since internal Faraday rotation is suppressed in a pure electron--positron plasma, the data favour a dominant electron--proton component. Interpreting the characteristic Faraday thickness as internal rotation, and anchoring the magnetic-field and size scales with synchrotron self-absorption arguments, we infer a characteristic Faraday-rotating mass of order $M_{\rm rot}\sim10^{21}{\rm\,g}$, corresponding to only a small fraction, $f_{\rm rot}\sim10^{-3}$, of the accreted mass available during the flare. These results show that time-domain spectropolarimetry can turn transient Faraday complexity into a diagnostic of jet composition, mass loading, and plasma evolution in X-ray binary outbursts, and potentially other transient jetted sources.

AI.tldr: This paper uses MeerKAT L-band spectropolarimetry of the black hole X-ray binary during its 2023 outburst to analyze transient Faraday-complex structure associated with radio flares, finding that internal Faraday rotation favors an electron-proton jet plasma over electron-positron, and estimating the Faraday-rotating mass as ~10^21 g, which is only ~10^-3 of the accreted mass during the flare.
AI.motivation: Radio emission from X-ray binary outbursts is dominated by synchrotron radiation from relativistic jets but is usually studied only via total-intensity diagnostics. Spectropolarimetry provides a complementary probe of the magneto-ionic plasma through Faraday rotation and depolarisation, yet this approach is rarely applied to transient jetted sources.
AI.method: MeerKAT L-band spectropolarimetry was applied to the black hole X-ray binary during its 2023 outburst. Multiple spectropolarimetric techniques were used to identify transient Faraday-complex structure coincident with major radio flares, and the characteristic Faraday thickness was interpreted as internal rotation, with magnetic-field and size scales anchored via synchrotron self-absorption arguments.
AI.result: Transient Faraday-complex structure was found to be temporally associated with major radio flares, favoring a local (jet) origin over ISM or external screen origins. The data favor a dominant electron-proton jet plasma composition. The inferred Faraday-rotating mass is ~10^21 g, only ~10^-3 of the accreted mass available during the flare.
AI.conclusion: Time-domain spectropolarimetry can turn transient Faraday complexity into a diagnostic of jet composition, mass loading, and plasma evolution in X-ray binary outbursts and potentially other transient jetted sources.

title: Widespread Detection of Aromatic and Aliphatic Emission in the Dual Quasar J0749+2255 at Cosmic Noon
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures; accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Based on JWST/MIRI integral field observations, we report a widespread detection of aromatic and aliphatic hydrocarbon emission at rest-frame 3.3 and 3.4 micron in SDSSJ074922.96+225511.7 (hereafter J0749+2255), a dual quasar at redshift z~2.17, corresponding to a cosmic age of ~3 billion years after the Big Bang, a time period known as the "cosmic noon" when star formation and black hole growth peak. With the 3.3 micron emission ascribed to aromatic C--H stretches of small PAH molecules and the 3.4 micron emission assigned to aliphatic C--H stretches of aliphatic sidegroups attached to PAHs, we utilize the observed intensities of the 3.3 and 3.4 micron emission bands to estimate the aliphatic fractions of PAHs and their variations across J0749+2255, which is, to our knowledge, the most distant object to date in which both aromatics and aliphatics have ever been detected. We find that both the 3.3 and 3.4 micron emission bands are pronounced and the aliphatic fractions are surprisingly high in the most luminous regions centered on the two quasar nuclei, suggesting that not only small PAHs (of ~20--30 carbon atoms) but also their attached aliphatic sidegroups survive in intense ultraviolet radiation arising from extreme starburst.

AI.tldr: JWST/MIRI detects aromatic (3.3 μm) and aliphatic (3.4 μm) hydrocarbon emission in a dual quasar at z~2.17 (cosmic noon), finding surprisingly high aliphatic fractions near the quasar nuclei, indicating that both small PAHs (~20-30 C atoms) and their aliphatic sidegroups survive intense UV radiation from extreme starbursts—the most distant detection of both species to date.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether aromatic and aliphatic hydrocarbon emissions can survive in the intense ultraviolet radiation fields near quasar nuclei at high redshift (cosmic noon, ~3 Gyr after Big Bang), using J0749+2255 as a testbed.
AI.method: JWST/MIRI integral field observations of rest-frame 3.3 μm (aromatic C–H stretches of small PAHs) and 3.4 μm (aliphatic C–H stretches of aliphatic sidegroups) emission bands; intensity ratios used to derive aliphatic fractions of PAHs and map their spatial variations across the dual quasar system.
AI.result: Both 3.3 and 3.4 μm bands are widespread and pronounced; aliphatic fractions are surprisingly high in the most luminous regions centered on the two quasar nuclei, indicating survival of small PAHs (~20–30 C atoms) and their aliphatic attachments under extreme starburst UV radiation. This represents the most distant detection of both aromatics and aliphatics.
AI.conclusion: Small PAHs and their aliphatic sidegroups can persist in harsh quasar environments at cosmic noon, challenging the expectation that such molecules would be destroyed by intense UV fields, and providing new constraints on hydrocarbon chemistry in the early universe.

title: Geminga and Monogem in the CTAO Era: Probing TeV Halos and Cosmic-Ray Transport
summary: TeV halos around Geminga and Monogem (B0656+14) reveal regions of strongly suppressed diffusion near middle-aged pulsars. Determining the sizes and magnetic-field strengths of these slow-diffusion zones is important for modelling lepton transport and assessing their contribution to the local positron excess. The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) will provide arcminute-scale imaging of extended gamma-ray emission. We construct two-zone diffusion models for Geminga and Monogem with GALPROP v57, injecting electrons and positrons according to the pulsar spin-down history and following their propagation through an evolving slow-diffusion bubble and the ambient interstellar medium. Calibrating to HAWC and Fermi-LAT measurements, we forward-fold the models through official CTAO instrument response functions, including realistic diffuse and instrumental backgrounds. For 50 h observations, both halos are detected with high significance ($\sim 13$--$30,σ$) from either site. Under optimistic background assumptions, CTAO can distinguish changes of $Δγ_1 \simeq 0.2$ in the high-energy injection index and $ΔB \simeq 2,μ{\rm G}$ in magnetic-field strength. For Monogem, compact bubbles with $R_{\rm SDZ}\approx30,{\rm pc}$ can be distinguished from extended ($\gtrsim50,{\rm pc}$) cases, although very large bubbles remain degenerate because of the finite field of view. Using an alternative Galactic diffuse template in the fit changes detection significances and parameter sensitivities by $\lesssim10%$, indicating robustness against plausible diffuse-background mismodelling.

AI.tldr: This paper simulates how CTAO will observe TeV halos around Geminga and Monogem, predicting high-significance detections and the ability to constrain diffusion zone sizes, magnetic field strengths, and injection spectra, with robustness against diffuse background uncertainties.
AI.motivation: TeV halos around middle-aged pulsars show strongly suppressed diffusion, but their sizes and magnetic field strengths remain poorly constrained. Measuring these parameters is crucial for modeling lepton transport and understanding the local positron excess.
AI.method: Two-zone diffusion models for Geminga and Monogem are constructed using GALPROP v57, injecting electrons/positrons based on pulsar spin-down history and propagating through an evolving slow-diffusion bubble and ambient ISM. Models are calibrated to HAWC/Fermi-LAT data and forward-folded through official CTAO IRFs, including diffuse and instrumental backgrounds.
AI.result: Both halos are detected with high significance (~13-30σ) in 50 h observations. CTAO can distinguish Δγ₁ ≈ 0.2 in injection index and ΔB ≈ 2 μG in magnetic field. For Monogem, compact bubbles (~30 pc) can be distinguished from extended (≥50 pc) cases. Using alternative diffuse templates changes results by <10%.
AI.conclusion: CTAO will provide sensitive, robust measurements of pulsar TeV halos, enabling precise characterization of slow-diffusion zones that are key to understanding cosmic-ray transport and the positron excess.

title: Ultraviolet Interstellar Extinction toward High Galactic Latitudes
comment: 28 pages, 13 figures, 3 tables; accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Nearby high Galactic latitude clouds provide a unique laboratory to study the physics and structure of the Galactic interstellar medium (ISM) and the properties of the interstellar dust. In this work, we select 32 sightlines toward reddened background stars at high Galactic latitudes with |b| > 20 degr, for which high-quality spectra from the International Ultraviolet Explorer are available. We utilize the "pair-method" to derive the ultraviolet interstellar extinction curves for these sightlines. We examine the extinction properties of these sightlines and find no systematic variations with the Galactic latitudes, although they do show appreciable sightline-to-sightline variations.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes ultraviolet interstellar extinction curves toward 32 high Galactic latitude sightlines using IUE data, finding sightline-to-sightline variations but no systematic dependence on Galactic latitude.
AI.motivation: High Galactic latitude clouds offer a unique opportunity to study the physics and structure of the Galactic interstellar medium (ISM) and interstellar dust properties away from the complex Galactic plane.
AI.method: Selected 32 sightlines toward reddened background stars at |b| > 20° with high-quality IUE spectra, and applied the pair-method to derive ultraviolet interstellar extinction curves.
AI.result: No systematic variations in extinction properties with Galactic latitude were found, though significant sightline-to-sightline variations were observed.
AI.conclusion: High-latitude ISM exhibits heterogeneous dust extinction properties independent of latitude, implying local environmental factors dominate over large-scale Galactic structure.

title: The emergence of X-ray emission lines during relativistic radio-jet formation in the changing-look active galactic nucleus 1ES 1927+654
summary: We present results from a comprehensive multi-wavelength monitoring campaign of the changing-look active galactic nucleus 1ES 1927+654 during the onset and evolution of a radio jet (May 2022-August 2025). Using observations from XMM-Newton, Swift, TNG, ZTF, VLA, and VLBA, we characterize the spectral evolution of the source. Soft X-ray emission lines at ~0.56 keV and ~1 keV have appeared with variable strength and width during the formation of a nascent jet, with the ~1 keV feature persisting since the post-2017 flare phase. We also report the detection of a broad (~800 eV) Fe K emission feature at ~(6-7) keV in ~70 ks of stacked EPIC-pn spectra, marking the first such detection in this historically featureless source. Joint spectral fitting of XMM-Newton EPIC-pn and RGS data reveals the presence of ionized absorbers in 2022, followed by weaker absorption from 2023 to 2025. The emergence of emission features concurrent with the decline of ionized absorption suggests a transition in the inner accretion and outflow processes, indicating the reflection and reprocessing of X-rays from the inner accretion disk during jet formation. The apparent weakening of ionized outflows as the jet develops supports a scenario in which accreting material is preferentially channeled into the jet rather than expelled as winds. Furthermore, both the 0.3-2 keV soft X-ray and 5 GHz radio fluxes, which have increased by factors of ~10 and ~60, respectively, since 2022, have recently plateaued at elevated levels. Combined with steady optical emission, this indicates a stabilized accretion disk, corona, and jet configuration. Finally, the absence of broad optical emission lines suggests that the broad-line region is either not along our line of sight or insufficiently illuminated by the central source.

AI.tldr: Multi-wavelength monitoring (2022-2025) of the changing-look AGN 1ES 1927+654 reveals the emergence of soft X-ray emission lines, a broad Fe K feature, and evolving ionized absorbers during jet formation, suggesting a transition from wind-dominated outflows to jet-dominated accretion, with stabilized disk-corona-jet configuration since 2022.
AI.motivation: To characterize the spectral evolution of 1ES 1927+654 during the onset and evolution of a radio jet, and to understand the interplay between accretion flows, outflows, and jet formation in changing-look AGNs.
AI.method: Comprehensive multi-wavelength monitoring campaign using XMM-Newton, Swift, TNG, ZTF, VLA, and VLBA from May 2022 to August 2025; joint spectral fitting of EPIC-pn and RGS data; analysis of soft X-ray emission lines, Fe K features, and ionized absorbers.
AI.result: Soft X-ray emission lines at ~0.56 keV and ~1 keV emerged with variable profiles; first detection of a broad Fe K line (~800 eV) at ~6-7 keV; ionized absorbers present in 2022 weakened by 2023-2025; soft X-ray and 5 GHz radio fluxes increased by ~10x and ~60x respectively, then plateaued; no broad optical emission lines detected.
AI.conclusion: The emergence of emission features concurrent with declining absorption indicates a transition from ionized outflows to reflection/reprocessing during jet formation. Weakening winds as the jet develops suggest accreting material is channeled into the jet rather than expelled. The plateauing of X-ray and radio fluxes alongside stable optical emission points to a stabilized accretion disk, corona, and jet configuration.

title: A Model Context Protocol Server for Astrophysical RAG: Unified Access to HI, Dwarf, Globular Cluster, IntZ, and ALPINE Kinematic Corpora with FAISS Semantic Search
comment: 10 Pages 3 Tables 1 figure
summary: We present the EPS Research Astro-RAG MCP Server v2.3.0, a cross-platform Model Context Protocol (MCP) implementation providing unified, machine-readable access to five astrophysical corpora spanning the local universe (z = 0) to z = 5.68 (the high-redshift frontier of the ALPINE survey). The server exposes a humanreadable browser query interface, a REST API, and an LLM-native MCP endpoint, enabling deterministic retrieval, metadata filtering, and structured analysis across 2,064 objects: galaxies spanning HI rotation curve surveys, dwarf and irregular systems, and high-redshift kinematic targets, together with Milky Way globular clusters. Version 2.3.0 introduces FAISS-accelerated natural-language similarity search using pre-built 384-dimensional MiniLM-L6-v2 vector indexes, enabling corpus-wide semantic queries without fine-tuning or API keys. We describe the server architecture, unified schema design, FAISS index construction pipeline, MCP toolset, and cross-epoch use cases including rotation-curve retrieval, metadata filtering, and semantic similarity exploration. The server is publicly deployed on HuggingFace Spaces (https://dflynn5656-astro-rag-mcp.hf.space), released under the MIT License, and fully reproducible from Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21154451). The full platform is available at https://github.com/eps-research/rag-corpus-series.

AI.tldr: The paper presents EPS Research Astro-RAG MCP Server v2.3.0, a cross-platform system providing unified access to five astrophysical datasets (2,064 objects from z=0 to z=5.68) via browser, REST API, and LLM-native MCP endpoint, with FAISS-accelerated semantic search using MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings.
AI.motivation: To create a unified, machine-readable access point for diverse astrophysical datasets spanning a wide redshift range, enabling deterministic retrieval, metadata filtering, and structured analysis without requiring fine-tuning or API keys.
AI.method: Built as a cross-platform Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with three access interfaces (browser, REST API, LLM-native MCP endpoint). Uses FAISS-accelerated natural-language similarity search with pre-built 384-dimensional MiniLM-L6-v2 vector indexes. Implements unified schema design and metadata filtering across five astrophysical corpora.
AI.result: The server is publicly deployed on HuggingFace Spaces, released under MIT License, fully reproducible from Zenodo, and covers 2,064 objects including galaxies with HI rotation curves, dwarf/irregular systems, high-redshift kinematic targets, and Milky Way globular clusters.
AI.conclusion: The server enables cross-epoch use cases such as rotation-curve retrieval, metadata filtering, and semantic similarity exploration across datasets spanning from local universe (z=0) to high-redshift frontier (z=5.68).

title: The disk luminosity deficit as a tracer of receding disk during Soft-to-Hard transitions in Black Hole X-ray Binaries
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: Tracing the evolution of the thin accretion disk during the soft-to-hard state transition in black hole X-ray binaries (BHXRBs) remains difficult because conventional spectral estimates of the disk inner radius become highly model-dependent once the thermal component weakens. We present evidence that the thin disk recedes during this transition, obtained from a systematic study of RXTE/PCA observations of 26 BHXRBs. In 24 outbursts, the disk luminosity decays exponentially in the soft state, then drops significantly below the extrapolated baseline. This thermal luminosity deficit is considered a signature of reduced accretion efficiency, caused by the outward receding of the optically thick disk. Under this framework, we found that the estimated characteristic truncation radius increases rapidly as the systems evolve through the soft-to-hard transition. This interpretation is supported by timing analysis: in observations with well-constrained power density spectra, the characteristic frequencies of broadband noise and low-frequency QPOs generally decrease as the inferred truncation radius increases, consistent with the expansion of a hot inner flow. The onset and rapidity of recession vary substantially across different sources and outbursts. Our results demonstrate that luminosity deficits provide a practical empirical tracer of thin disk receding during soft-to-hard transitions, when direct spectral radius measurements become unreliable.

AI.tldr: Using RXTE/PCA data from 26 BHXRBs, the study shows that the thin accretion disk recedes during soft-to-hard state transitions, identified by a luminosity deficit below the exponential decay baseline. This deficit indicates reduced accretion efficiency from disk truncation, with the characteristic truncation radius increasing as the transition progresses. Timing analysis supports this by showing decreasing characteristic frequencies with larger inferred truncation radii, consistent with an expanding hot inner flow.
AI.motivation: Tracing the evolution of the thin accretion disk during soft-to-hard state transitions in BHXRBs remains difficult because conventional spectral estimates of the disk inner radius become highly model-dependent once the thermal component weakens.
AI.method: Systematic study of RXTE/PCA observations of 26 BHXRBs; analysis of disk luminosity decay in 24 outbursts; estimation of characteristic truncation radius from thermal luminosity deficit; timing analysis of broadband noise and low-frequency QPOs.
AI.result: The disk luminosity decays exponentially in the soft state, then drops significantly below the extrapolated baseline during the transition. The estimated characteristic truncation radius increases rapidly as systems evolve through the soft-to-hard transition. Characteristic frequencies of broadband noise and low-frequency QPOs generally decrease as the inferred truncation radius increases. The onset and rapidity of recession vary substantially across different sources and outbursts.
AI.conclusion: Luminosity deficits provide a practical empirical tracer of thin disk receding during soft-to-hard transitions, when direct spectral radius measurements become unreliable.

title: Assembly bias from nuisance to probe I: the relation between galactic conformity and the linear matter clustering
comment: Letter submitted to A&A -- Comments welcome
summary: Two-halo galactic conformity is commonly interpreted as a manifestation of galaxy assembly bias, but its statistical structure and physical origin remain unclear. We aim to write the quenched-neighbour statistic in correlation-function form, test whether its scale dependence follows the linear matter correlation function $ξ_{\rm mm}^{\rm lin}(r)$, and separate the contributions of halo-mass bias and assembly bias to its amplitude. Using galaxies in IllustrisTNG300-1 at $z=0$, we measure the two-halo galactic conformity statistic of quenched neighbours at distance $r$, $Δf_Q(r)$, and related quantities in real space, compute the required correlations, perform shuffling tests at fixed halo mass, compare several $Δf$ observables, and explore the transformed family $G_n$. We show explicitly that $Δf_Q(r)$ can be written directly in terms of correlation functions and that, over $\sim 2$-$40\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$, it is well described by $A_{\rm fit}\,ξ_{\rm mm}^{\rm lin}(r)$. Thus nonlinear and baryonic terms do not dominate the residual scale dependence isolated by this statistic. Halo-mass bias alone predicts lower amplitudes than measured, while fixed-mass shuffling strongly suppresses the signal; in TNG300 the amplitude is therefore dominated by %fixed-mass assembly-dependent occupancy. galaxy assembly bias at fixed halo mass. Quenching, colour, and concentration share a common rescaled shape, whereas stellar-mass and halo-mass splits do not. These results suggest that galaxy assembly bias sets the amplitude of two-halo conformity, while the double-difference structure of the statistic suppresses nonlinear residuals when the compared populations have similar halo-mass and transition-scale structure.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that two-halo galactic conformity (measured as Δf_Q(r)) can be expressed as a correlation function and follows the linear matter correlation function ξ_mm^lin(r) over ~2-40 h⁻¹Mpc. The amplitude is dominated by galaxy assembly bias at fixed halo mass, not merely halo-mass bias. Quenching, colour, and concentration share a common rescaled shape.
